articles.title_orig: Xinhua Headlines: China's search for U.S. airmen lost along Hump Route keeps WWII bonds alive
articles.title_zh: Xinhua Headlines: China's search for U.S. airmen lost along Hump Route keeps WWII bonds alive
articles.content_orig:
* Chinese and U.S. representatives held a ceremony in southwest China's Chengdu recently to hand over the remains of U.S. airmen who went missing along the Hump Route while helping China fight Japanese aggression during World War II (WWII).
* More than 1,000 Chinese and American aircrew members lost their lives along the route. The air corridor across the Himalayas became a vital lifeline for Allied supplies supporting China's resistance against Japanese aggression from 1942 to 1945.
* China and the United States have cooperated in searching for American military personnel missing during WWII since the 1970s. At the ceremony, a Chinese official said that China has long supported the search on humanitarian grounds and is willing to continue practical cooperation with the United States in this field.
CHENGDU, Nov. 15 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese honor guards carried a box containing human remains to a table and carefully set it down. U.S. Chief Warrant Officer Christine Bilas then gently placed a folded American national flag on top of this box.
"Bring them home," said U.S. Navy Captain Colin Alexander Eliot, a forensic expert with the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA), as he watched the transfer ceremony at Jianchuan Museum in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, on Tuesday. U.S. Navy Commander Gregory Pavone then lifted the box from the table.
Inside the box were eight bone fragments recovered from a glacier more than 5,000 meters above sea level in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Believed to be the remains of American airmen who went missing while helping China fight Japanese aggression during World War II (WWII), these bone fragments had lain in the mountains for more than 80 years. Their identities have yet to be confirmed.
The handover followed three expeditions over more than two years by a Chinese civilian search team, part of a decades-long effort by China and the United States to account for missing American military personnel.
THREE TRIPS TO THE GLACIER
Cering Qoizha, deputy curator of Jianchuan Museum's branch in Chongqing, southwest China, set out in 2024 to search for wartime aircraft wreckage and human remains in the glaciers of Nyingchi, Xizang.
A Tibetan from Sichuan's Garze Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture, he enlisted his two elder brothers and several local guides for these expeditions.
The first attempt was cut short by a damaged cable crossing over a river. After the crossing was rebuilt, the team returned and found aircraft wreckage. It was not until their third trip that they discovered the bone fragments.
The journey took them through forests and swamps, across icy rivers and up steep cliffs, where bears, hidden crevasses and ice holes posed constant dangers.
On the glacier, decades of freezing and thawing had left the remains trapped beneath rocks.
"We could only lie on the ground and use our hands and branches to turn over the rocks and search carefully," Cering Qoizha recalled. The team eventually recovered eight fragments.
He had led an earlier expedition that found American aircrew remains in Xizang in 2015.
"The crews of the Hump Route gave their lives to support China's resistance against Japanese aggression and lay alone on the glaciers for decades," Cering Qoizha said. "They were heroes. Bringing them back from the glaciers is something I wanted to do, and something I should do."
After Japanese forces occupied Myanmar in 1942 and cut off the Yunnan-Myanmar road, which was China's last major overland supply link to the outside world, China and the United States established air routes connecting the state of Assam in northeastern India with Kunming in southwest China.
Known as the Hump Route, this air corridor across the Himalayas became a vital lifeline for Allied supplies supporting China's resistance against Japanese aggression from 1942 to 1945.
The route featured snow-covered mountains, deep gorges, glaciers and tropical forests. Violent air currents, low air pressure, hail, freezing weather conditions and attacks by Japanese aircraft made the journey perilous. So many planes crashed along the route that crews came to call it the "Aluminum Trail."
More than 1,000 Chinese and American aircrew lost their lives along the route. With the high mountains and glaciers making searches exceptionally difficult, many of their remains have never been recovered.
"Every day felt like the last," Chinese pilot Zhou Bing, who flew more than 110 round trips along the route, once recalled. Friends who were together one day could be gone the next, he said.
The airlift also depended on the labor and sacrifices of ordinary Chinese people.
At Jianchuan Museum, enormous stone rollers weighing between eight and 15 tonnes recall the construction of wartime airfields in Sichuan and Yunnan, both in China's southwest. Without access to modern road rollers, dozens or even hundreds of workers had to pull these heavy stones to prepare runways. Some were injured or killed while working under harsh wartime conditions.
Chinese military personnel and civilians also monitored Japanese aircraft movements, providing American forces with information on their numbers, types, altitudes and directions when ground radar coverage was limited.
For Fan Jianchuan, curator of the privately run Jianchuan Museum, searching for the missing American airmen is a way of repaying a debt of gratitude.
"When a country, or a person, faces the greatest danger and hardship, having friends come to help is very important," he said.
The museum began searching for wartime aircraft wreckage in Sichuan more than 20 years ago, later extending its expeditions to the remote glaciers of Xizang.
"The Hump Route crews deserve to be remembered and thanked forever," Fan said. "In practical terms, that means finding their remains in China and returning them to the American side."
China and the United States have cooperated in searching for American military personnel missing during WWII since the 1970s. In 2008, China's Ministry of National Defense and the U.S. Department of Defense signed a memorandum of understanding in Shanghai, establishing a formal mechanism for this work.
At Tuesday's ceremony, an official with the general office of the Central Military Commission (CMC) said the joint efforts to recover the remains of missing U.S. servicemen were a testament to the two countries' history of fighting side by side against Japanese fascism during WWII.
China has long supported the search on humanitarian grounds and is willing to continue practical cooperation with the United States in this field, the official said, adding that such efforts could contribute positively to building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability.
Another official with the Office for International Military Cooperation of the CMC said investigation and joint working teams had conducted surveys and excavations in more than 100 locations across China, drawing support from local governments and residents.
As the wartime stories of the Flying Tigers and Hump Route became more widely known, growing numbers of Chinese civilians joined the searches, the official said, citing Jianchuan Museum as a notable example.
The official said the expanding involvement of ordinary people echoed the two countries' wartime cooperation and showed that "the hope of China-U.S. relations lies in the people."
Pavone also spoke of the longstanding cooperation.
"These joint efforts have been going on for decades and are one of the most durable areas of cooperation between our two militaries," he said, thanking the museum, local authorities and Chinese military and diplomatic agencies for their contributions.
The remains still await identification. After the remains reach the United States, the DPAA will conduct DNA testing, examine historical evidence, and compare military records. Families will be notified only after identification is confirmed.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang, Alice Huang and China spy allegation: Who benefits from the controversy?
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang, Alice Huang and China spy allegation: Who benefits from the controversy?
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Jensen Huang and President Trump at a 2025 White House event. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence.
Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House.
The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice.
Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation.
Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO.
The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public.
Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia.
What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight.

articles.title_orig: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.title_zh: Study Hard, Get a Career and Get Ahead? It’s Not What It Used to Be.
articles.content_orig:
Protest movements have long relied on students as some of the most ardent foot soldiers. Young people have been on the front lines of protests against war, climate change and racial inequality. But in huge protests that have shaken India and France this fall, students have revolted against the failed promises of education itself.
In India, students took to the streets after the government abruptly canceled the results of a medical-school admissions exam because test questions had been leaked online. Aspiring doctors had to take the test again, after many spent years studying for up to 12 hours a day in hopes of winning one of the coveted spots — and the chance of upward mobility. Young people across the country saw the scandal as emblematic of a broken education system and were furious.
In France, students in poor suburbs outside Paris began protesting the decrepit physical condition of their schools, an opaque university admissions system and absent teachers. French education had long promised to serve as a “social elevator” enabling young people to advance in society, but had fallen into disrepair. Soon, demonstrations spread across the country and, in some cities, spiraled into rioting.
In both countries, the anger of the students shows no signs of abating. And while in many ways France and India could hardly be more different, their unrest was sparked by a similar source of outrage: the breakdown of a foundational social contract that one could call the meritocratic bargain.
It is a promise that lies at the core of many countries’ political compacts. Though specifics can vary, the central proposition usually goes something like this: A fair society rewards merit. Educational achievements are a good measure of merit because education is open to all and leads to valuable skills. Therefore, education should be a route to social and economic advancement.
The value of this system is not just that it selects for those with high ability, but also that it offers a justification for the resulting socioeconomic hierarchy — including who ends up at the bottom. “All selection mechanisms generate losers,” said Nicholas Kuipers, a professor at Princeton University who studies the politics of meritocracy. “The question is, Who do you want to be a loser, and who do you want to be a winner?”

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Service Restored After Widespread Outage, Company Says
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Service Restored After Widespread Outage, Company Says
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X , the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."
The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X . "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.
"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."
Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."
"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account .
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024 .
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.
"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.
Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.
Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.
Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.
IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as it launches internal probe into reports about its business
articles.content_orig:
Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.
The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.
U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.
"Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.
Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.
The company, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.
Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation."
"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.
The company added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump to meet Xi, Putin in historic three-way talks in China on November 19
articles.title_zh: Trump to meet Xi, Putin in historic three-way talks in China on November 19
articles.content_orig:

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand: Alleged rape victim wants age of consent law changed
articles.content_orig:
A woman who alleges that she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity and is campaigning for a staggered age of consent in an interview with the Sunday Times.
Mia Latter was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. She was known under the pseudonym 'Alice'. Brand denied the allegations at the time.
None of the women in the 2023 media investigation were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.
Reacting to the proposal, Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh said it would be a "massive step" to change the age of consent law, but that it "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny".
Speaking to the Sunday Times, she added that it was "disgusting" that a culture existed in the 2000s that "normalised and celebrated" celebrities having relationships with teenagers.
On Monday the entertainer was sentenced to 10 and a half years for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
The Sunday Times reported that Latter had initially described the allegation about Brand to them as a sexual assault and that is how they reported it in their 2023 investigation.
Latter, 37, "now calls this allegation rape", the paper said.
Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time, when she was on her way home from a shopping trip. She said Brand was working at MTV.
She told the paper: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power]."
She said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.
It was towards the end of their relationship that Latter was allegedly orally raped by Brand, according to the Sunday Times.
Latter said that she was now campaigning for the introduction of a "staggered" age of consent that would prohibit relationships between 16- and 17-year-olds and adults.
"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other," she told the paper. "If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to. But … if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."
She also told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.
In her interview with the Sunday Times she said that the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but the police wanted her to be part of a "subsequent trial".
A Met Police spokesperson said: "Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.
"Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.
"This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."
A spokesperson for the Crown Prosecution Service said it would "continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible".

articles.title_orig: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.title_zh: Turkish husband, who pushed pregnant wife off cliff, released from prison 6 years into life sentence
articles.content_orig:
A Turkish man sentenced to life in prison for pushing his pregnant wife to her death off a famed 1,000-foot cliff for a life insurance policy payout was set free after only six years, sparking intense backlash.
Hakan Aysal was freed from a high-security prison as Turkey’s Supreme Court’s Criminal General Assembly reviews an appeal on the convicted killer’s lifetime sentence for the 2018 death of his wife, Semra Aysal, Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet reported Friday.
“My client’s six years of unjust imprisonment, approximately four of which he spent in solitary confinement, has come to an end,” Aysal’s lawyer said, according to the outlet.
Aysal, 45, was serving an aggravated life imprisonment sentence for the premeditated killing of his 32-year-old wife, whom he shoved off the scenic Butterfly Valley cliff after taking selfies together.
Aysal was convicted in October 2022.
Aysal’s lawyers and Supreme Court Chief Prosecutor Ömer Taş claimed there was a lack of sufficient, convincing evidence to convict the killer husband.
Turkish prosecutors had argued that Aysal shoved his wife, who was seven months pregnant with the couple’s child, while they were at the popular destination near the city of Muğla in southwestern Turkey.
Prosecutors told the court that Aysal had taken out a $25,000 accident insurance policy in his wife’s name, making himself the sole beneficiary and collecting the funds immediately after her death.
Aysal – who once attempted to enter a plea of insanity – has maintained his innocence, claiming he never pushed his wife and instead she had disappeared after he turned his back on her for a second.
A witness, who had recorded a video capturing the final moments of Semra Aysal on the cliff, said the husband had appeared “unusually calm” after the incident.
“We even joked, ‘Either this man will throw the woman off or the woman will throw the man.’ There was no interaction between them,'” witness Recep Sahin told police after he shared the footage with them.
Pro-women rights groups were outraged following the court’s decision to release Aysal as they review his appeal.
“The decision is extremely worrying, not only for this case but also in terms of the evaluation of evidence in femicide cases and the debates surrounding impunity,” lawyer Hediye Gökçe Baykal told Cumhuriyet.
The women’s wing of the New Party, Turkey’s social democratic political faction, called for justice for both Semra Aysal and her unborn child.
“A woman and her seven-month-old unborn baby lost their lives. The defendant, who received an aggravated life sentence, is now free,” the party wrote, according to the outlet.
“The Supreme Court has issued a release order for Hakan Aysal, who was sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for being responsible for the death of his wife, Semra Aysal, in Muğla. We ask: How will accountability be provided for the deaths of Semra and her unborn baby?” the group questioned.

Volodymyr Zelensky has accused SpaceX of hampering Ukraine’s defences by maintaining speed restrictions on its Starshield satellite terminals in Russian-occupied territory.
The limits, which Ukraine says have been in place for five days, are making it harder for its forces to intercept Russian jet-powered drones before they reach Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky dismissed the company's explanation that the restrictions were caused by a “technical issue”, telling reporters on Saturday: “We do not believe that is the case.”
He warned that limiting the service in occupied territory carried political implications, adding: “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporarily occupied territories as not ours.”
SpaceX has denied imposing restrictions or changing its satellite operations.
Zelensky also revealed that US negotiators had asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from Donbas in exchange for Nato membership during talks in Abu Dhabi. “This was the first time this had been raised,” he said, insisting Kyiv would not surrender its territory.
America’s approach to peace in Ukraine is beset with double standards and hypocrisy, writes Keir Giles. Hesitation and weakness will be seized upon by Russia – making the situation worse, not better
A large fire broke out at an industrial facility in Nizhnekamsk, in Russia’s Tatarstan region, overnight on Saturday, amid reports of a Ukrainian drone attack on the city’s industrial zone.
Residents reported seeing drones and an attack on one of the facilities, while footage shared by Osint showed a large blaze with several fires burning across the industrial area. The Telegram channel Exilenova+ identified the SIBUR-owned Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical complex as a likely target.
The plant, around 1,200km from Ukraine, produces synthetic rubber, plastics and other petrochemical products.
Russia has claimed that its forces struck a cargo vessel and port infrastructure in Chornomorsk, in Ukraine’s Odesa region, on Saturday.
The Russian defence ministry said the vessel was being used to transport supplies for the Ukrainian military and that facilities used to unload military cargo had also been hit, according to state news agency RIA Novosti.
US negotiators have asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for joining Nato, president Zelensky has said.
“The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He insisted Kyiv was not prepared to surrender its territory, but said he would put the question to a national referendum if Ukraine received a comprehensive security package, including firm guarantees, a strong and properly funded military, and money for reconstruction.
Zelensky said the proposal meant Nato membership was “back on the agenda”, but acknowledged that reaching an agreement would be difficult given Vladimir Putin’s opposition to Ukraine joining the alliance.
Volodymyr Zelensky has accused SpaceX of maintaining speed restrictions on Starshield, its military-focused satellite communications system, saying they are leaving Ukrainian forces less able to intercept Russian drones.
The restrictions have been in place for five days, with terminals in Russian-occupied territory capped at 161km/h, he said.
“We do not believe that is the case," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday, rejecting SpaceX’s explanation that the problem was technical.
He also warned that restricting the service in occupied territory amounted to partially recognising those areas as no longer Ukrainian. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognising the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he said.
Ukraine’s envoy in Washington Denys Sienik told RFE that the restrictions were widespread. SpaceX has denied making any changes to its service.

articles.title_orig: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.title_zh: Saudi-led coalition intercepts suspected Houthi missiles and drones
articles.content_orig:
Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said they intercepted two missiles and five drones targeting different parts of the country, allegedly launched by the Iran-backed rebel group.
“Air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards Riyadh,” Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, said in a post on X early on Sunday.
He said the coalition forces also shot down three drones in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern region on Sunday.
Earlier on Saturday, al-Maliki said two suspected Houthi drones “were intercepted and destroyed” in the Riyadh and southern regions.
Meanwhile, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), claimed to have shot down an armed Saudi coalition reconnaissance aircraft carrying out “hostile operations in the airspace of al-Jawf”.
In a post on X, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the Iran-aligned group was able to “repel a number of Saudi military formations using several Yemeni-made surface-to-air missiles” and that it was the fifth aircraft the Houthis had shot down since the escalation began.
At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to the kingdom’s authorities.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, as well as the East-West pipeline and oil infrastructure in eastern and southern Saudi Arabia.
The interceptions come as the Saudi-led forces supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government also said they intercepted several drones launched towards the Yemeni city of Marib.
Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said government forces had made gains against the Houthis during heavy fighting in the al-Hazm and Madghal districts of al-Jawf, as fighting intensified in Marib.
Al-Nuzaili said 321 Houthi leaders had been killed or wounded in 723 targeted operations by Saudi-backed forces in the Taiz, Lahij, Marib and al-Jawf governorates, and that 117 military vehicles used by the Iran-allied rebel group had been destroyed.
The coalition carried out at least 37 air strikes and 56 drone attacks, as well as 541 artillery strikes.
Houthi spokesman Saree said the Saudi-led coalition had launched 72 air strikes against the Houthis in the Saada, Taiz, Lahij and al-Jawf governorates over the past 24 hours.
He said the Houthis targeted Yemen’s Saudi-backed forces in the Kharaz area of the Lahij governorate with ballistic missiles.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported that two women and two children were injured as a result of artillery shelling by Saudi-backed forces in a residential neighbourhood of the Shuaub district in Sanaa, Yemen’s capital controlled by the Houthis.
More than 340,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting in Yemen since August, according to the International Organization for Migration.
As the fight between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis escalated, the US Embassy in Riyadh issued a nationwide security alert on Saturday urging Americans in the kingdom to exercise “heightened vigilance”, citing an increased threat of Houthi attacks.
The embassy said Houthi attacks on airports and other critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia had “caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions”, warning that hostilities could spread “rapidly”.
“Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia,” it said.

articles.title_orig: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.title_zh: Could everything be broken? Grounded jets, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder
articles.content_orig:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.
Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.
At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.
It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.
The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.
Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.
The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.
When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.
Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?
First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”
Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.
Could that really be a coincidence?
Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.
For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?
Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers .
Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.
U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks , in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days . If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?
Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government cou

articles.title_orig: A Grizzly Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules Banff Park, and Draws a Crowd
articles.title_zh: A Grizzly Known as ‘the Boss’ Rules Banff Park, and Draws a Crowd
articles.content_orig:
“The Boss,” the near mythical grizzly bear king of Banff National Park. Credit... All in the Wild Photography
Reporting from Banff National Park, Canmore and Dead Man’s Flats, Alberta.
To the scientists and wardens of Banff National Park he is grizzly bear 122. But to everyone who lives in or near Canada’s oldest national park, and many of its 4.5 million annual visitors, he is the Boss.
He has been struck by a freight train without apparent ill effect. He has shrugged off being hit by cars. Scientists have confirmed that he killed and snacked on a black bear at least once, and he is believed to have fathered many, if not most, of the bears in his 2,000-square-kilometer territory.
Most of all, the Boss has become Canada’s 700-pound celebrity bear king. When he strolls along the Trans-Canada Highway looking for dandelions, “bear jams” swiftly follow. His battles with a rival bear known as Split Lip are legendary. (He caused the split lip.) His annual awakening from hibernation, usually in March, is reported by news outlets across Alberta.
Galleries in Banff and neighboring Canmore ship giant photos of him worldwide. His image appears on fridge magnets, T-shirts and tote bags. A local restaurant is named for him, its main dining room dominated by a scrap metal sculpture of the bear.
But despite his fearsome demeanor, enhanced by four-inch claws, few bear experts consider the Boss a threat to park visitors or residents. Rather, they fear his celebrity and the legions of fans it have created, may be the biggest threat to his life and his dominance.

articles.title_orig: FAA was warned for years about repair risks leading to nationwide ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA was warned for years about repair risks leading to nationwide ground stop
articles.content_orig:
There’s been finger-pointing, stranded travelers and shifting schedules as airlines race to clear backlogged flights.
Follow additional updates on impacts of the nationwide FAA ground stop here .
• Untangling the mess: Airlines spent the day re-routing stranded passengers , shuffling crew schedules and trying to clear the backlog of flights after yesterday’s rare nationwide ground stop. While delays and cancellations persisted Saturday, more flights are arriving on time and fewer were canceled for Sunday. The FAA administrator said he expects airlines to resume full schedules by the end of the weekend.
• What went wrong: The communication outages that forced the ground stop likely stemmed from upgrade work on a dated system, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, though he said it’s still unclear if contractor error or an equipment malfunction caused the meltdown.
• Blame game: While the Trump administration has yet to provide a precise explanation , Duffy publicly criticized the contractor involved in the upgrade work, suggesting L3Harris may have made mistakes. The defense contractor says it’s supporting the FAA’s investigation .
As airlines spent Saturday working through the backlog from Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said he expects carriers to return to full schedules by the end of the weekend .
Meanwhile, top House Democrats are questioning the administration’s request for more funding for air traffic control, and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul has called for Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign or be removed.
CNN’s Kaanita Iyer, René Marsh, Aleena Fayaz, Sydney Bishop, Molly English and Brian Todd, Maria Aguilar Prieto, Emma Tucker and Taylor Galgano contributed to this report.
Some cruise lines are also feeling the effects of Friday’s nationwide ground stop.
Princess Cruises said it delayed departures for three ships scheduled to sail from US ports on Saturday, giving passengers additional time to account for travel disruptions. The cruise line said the delays will not impact the ships’ itineraries.
Carnival Cruise Lines also pushed back some departure times on Saturday, a company spokesperson told CNN.
More than 6,200 flights within, into, or out of the United States have been canceled for Saturday and at least 760 are already canceled for Sunday, according to flight data tracker FlightAware .
More than 7,700 US flights were delayed Saturday, while at least another 200 Sunday flights had already been delayed.
As of 8 p.m. ET, Delta Air Lines had canceled 26% of its flights, American Airlines canceled 42% of its flights and United Airlines canceled 26% of its flights slated for Saturday.
The top Democrats on two House panels overseeing the aviation industry announced today that employees from the Federal Aviation Administration and Transportation Department will brief their staff on Monday, as questions swirl around the failures that led to Friday’s nationwide ground stop.
Monday’s briefing, the lawmakers said in a news release, will revolve around the Trump administration’s request for an additional $30 billion in funding to upgrade the US air traffic control system.
The representatives – Rick Larsen, ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and André Carson, ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation – expressed skepticism about the ask, adding that they expect to hear from Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford by an early December hearing.
Larson and Carson pointed to the $12.5 billion passed by Congress in June 2025 to update air traffic control systems.
“Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?” Larsen and Carson wrote.
Members from the Voyage Church band were supposed to get on a flight from the Miami International Airport to Guatemala for a mission trip, but just like many others, their flight was delayed.
The church band has been playing music while they wait out the delay.
“What we have seen is people around here are frustrated, they’re sad, but when we started singing, we brought light and smiles upon their faces, and it does encourage all of us,” Dave Njuguna, a member of Voyage Church’s band, told CNN’s Carolina Peguero on Saturday evening.
Student pilot Mosab Nadi was completing the third leg of his first solo cross-country flight in the Fort Worth, Texas, area when the nationwide ground stop happened Friday.
“Ma’am I’m a student pilot. Honestly, this is my first time doing solo cross country and I don’t know what to do,” Nadi is heard telling an air traffic controller in now-viral ATC audio.
Although Nadi had done takeoffs and landings by himself before, Friday was a crucial day: he was doing his first solo cross-country, meaning he would fly 150 nautical miles across three different airports by himself, he said.
The 32-year-old was about to land at Hicks Airfield after a successful three consecutive flights to complete the trip when he heard there was a ground stop.
“My initial thought was maybe there’s an accident at Hicks. There’s some type of incident and it’s not safe to land,” he said. “I mean it’s tough to imagine something like this would happen.”
At that point, Nadi said he decided to fly over the airport and above a nearby lake to have some time to communicate with air traffic control and figure out what was happening.
“The plane is going to be flying, right? But I mean, where is the plane going to take you? That’s why you need to stay ahead. You need to have a plan on what to do next,” Nadi said.
The initial panic heard in his voice came because the experience was new to Nadi, he said, but he quickly calculated that he had enough fuel to land at another airport if needed.
The controller then advises Nadi to land at Hicks in the ATC audio and explains the ground stop is nationwide, but adds that she cannot be the one to clear him for landing, as that needs to come from a different person. She advises him to switch to Hicks’ advisory frequency.
“It was a smooth, nice landing,” Nadi said. “I cannot believe what happened. Once I landed (at Hicks), I was like, ‘what’s going on?’”
Addressing the air traffic control communication issues that arose before the nationwide ground stop Friday will require clarity about what exactly occurred, former air traffic controller S. Todd Yeary said.
Air traffic control audio shows communication issues surfaced between the Chicago Air Route Traffic Control Center and an American Airlines flight before the ground stop was declared.
“American 2774, I think you have a stuck mic?” ATC can be heard saying. “2774 we got you. It’s in and out,” someone says before static is heard.
It’s unclear whether backup frequencies were utilized, Yeary told CNN.
“What typically happens is you’ve got a number of radio frequencies that will come into play, and if any one of the frequencies has a disruption, there are a number of backups to the same frequency that allows for the controller to switch the actual transmitter site from their actual sector,” he said.
Replacing outdated technology that officials have blamed for the meltdown will take extensive time and meticulous planning, Yeary said.
CNN’s Sharif Paget contributed to this report.
Travelers should expect additional delays and cancellations at New York airports this weekend as airlines rebound from yesterday’s nationwide ground stop, according to New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and Port Authority Executive Director Kathryn Garcia.
John F. Kennedy International Airport, LaGuardia Airport and New York Stewart International Airport had over 800 cancellations and more than 600 delays by the end of last night, the governor and Garcia said in the statement.
Today, nearly 300 flights out of JFK were canceled or delayed and over 200 out of LaGuardia, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking website. For tomorrow, 25 flights from JFK have been canceled or delayed so far, along with 15 at LaGuardia.

articles.title_orig: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: US envoy Kushner says he aims to broker Europe-Russia talks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
US envoy Jared Kushner has said he is working with Russia, Ukraine and Europe to advance peace talks to the next stage, including facilitating direct engagement between Europe and Moscow.
Kushner told reporters on Saturday that “both sides” – Kyiv and Moscow – know that compromises will be necessary to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, and that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were now working on the next steps.
US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s comments follow peace talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday that failed to reach a breakthrough on ending the war, but resulted in a prisoner exchange .
The prospect of Europe’s involvement in the talks has grown in recent weeks, with leaders agreeing on Friday to send five representatives of European countries to represent the bloc at future peace talks.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday he did not believe it was possible to think about European security “without Europe”.
The Kremlin has signalled openness to negotiations with Europe, but has criticised a lack of proposals from the bloc.
The five countries attending – France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom – have signalled a readiness to send troops as part of a “coalition of the willing” to secure Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire.
Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC, said that the Russian “acceptance, as it has been accepted by Jared Kushner of European participation [in the talks], is something that could actually be important”.
“Kushner makes direct reference as well to the issue of security guarantees required by Ukraine, and he makes clear that it would be NATO that would provide these guarantees,” Hanna said.
Moreover, he added, “as negotiators are suggesting, there might be another round of multilateral negotiations to build on what’s been called ‘substantial progress’ in the recent talks”.
In a lengthy post on X on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron said Europe must “state clearly” what it wants for the post-war period, “including to the Russians”.
Macron also stated his belief that Ukraine, which has Europe’s largest conventional army, has a key role to play in Europe’s post-war context alongside NATO, which he added is a “place where it fully belongs”.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that US negotiators had asked during the Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas, most of which Russia occupies, in exchange for joining NATO.
The war has raged while negotiations continue. November leaks from Russia’s official statistics agency showed that Moscow’s war effort has so far cost the lives of at least 450,000 soldiers.

articles.title_orig: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.title_zh: World leaders head to Asia for back-to-back diplomatic summits
articles.content_orig:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings
The global political centre of gravity will be firmly in Asia this week as world leaders fly in for back-to-back high-level summits against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.
Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .
The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .
Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.
The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.
Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.
“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”
Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.
While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.
Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.
The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.
For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.
The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.
Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.
Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.
“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.
Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.
China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.
Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.
A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .
Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.
Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo speaks of community 'suffering' on visit to remote Andes town
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has spoken about the "suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future", which he said had left communities under threat, during a visit to an isolated Andean village in his former diocese.
About 6,000 people live in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, located in a remote part of the Andes mountains of northern Peru, but the Pope's visit still drew a crowd of about 20,000, according to the Vatican.
At an outdoor Mass, the Pope spoke of "declining birth rates that are emptying villages" and the unequal distribution of the land's resources.
More than 40% of the population in the Cajamarca region, where the town is located, live in poverty - the highest figure in Peru, according to official data.
Cajamarca has lost the highest number of people to internal migration, with 729,000 people born there now living elsewhere in Peru.
In his sermon, the Pope thanked those who had made the journey to see him and emphasised the importance of never losing heart, despite life's difficulties.
The pontiff's Latin America tour comes roughly a month after he underwent surgery to remove part of his right lung after a cancerous lump was found during routine checks.
Santa Cruz is within the Diocese of Chiclayo, where the Pope served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. During his tenure, he visited Santa Cruz several times a year to minister to the town's rural population.
On Saturday, he returned by helicopter and was greeted by singing and cheering. He later did a tour in a popemobile, from which he waved to people who had travelled to see him.
Speaking at a local parish on Saturday, the 71-year-old said he felt "joy" at being able to visit the small town once again.
"It is like a very big dream that the Lord has allowed this servant to come here," he said.
Rev Kevin Noriega, who was ordained in 2018 by the then-bishop, told Reuters the visit had brought "enormous hope and emotion" to Santa Cruz.
He said: "People are eager to experience this Holy Mass ... because after so much time they will be able to see their bishop - 'Father Robert', as they used to call him - now as the Holy Father."
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the leader of the Catholic church, who was elected in May 2025.
The 12-day trip has included stops in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in Peru carries personal significance.
The US-born Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
The pontiff is set to leave Chiclayo on Sunday, when he will head to Cusco and then on to a Peruvian section of the Amazon rainforest. His tour of the region will conclude on Monday, at which point he will return to Rome.

articles.title_orig: 18 Years After Mumbai Massacre, Man Arrested for Spying on Chabad
articles.title_zh: 18 Years After Mumbai Massacre, Man Arrested for Spying on Chabad
articles.content_orig:
Nearly 18 years after the deadly terrorist attack on Mumbai’s Chabad House, India arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of gathering intelligence on the building. Full Story
Nearly 18 years after the deadly terrorist attack on Mumbai’s Chabad House, India arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of gathering intelligence on the building. Full Story
Indian authorities have arrested a 20-year-old man suspected of conducting surveillance of the Chabad House in Mumbai, nearly 18 years after the devastating terrorist attack that claimed the lives of Shluchim Rabbi Gabi and Rivky Holtzberg , HYD.
The suspect, identified as Yash Singh , a resident of Airoli in Navi Mumbai, was arrested on Saturday, November 14, following intelligence reports suggesting he was gathering sensitive information about Jewish institutions and individuals on behalf of foreign handlers.
According to Indian news outlets, including NDTV and The Times of India, Singh allegedly photographed sensitive locations, collected vehicle details and gathered precise geographical information about Jewish residents, businesses and foreign nationals in Mumbai.
The investigation reportedly began after Maharashtra’s Anti-Terrorism Squad (ATS) received information about Singh’s suspected connections to international criminal networks through social media.
Singh was initially detained by the ATS and subsequently arrested by police from the southern Indian state of Kerala in connection with an existing investigation under India’s Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act.
According to Indian police, Singh was allegedly instructed to conduct reconnaissance of sensitive locations in Mumbai, particularly the Chabad House, also known as Nariman House, in the Colaba neighborhood.
Investigators suspect that he received payments for gathering information and communicating with handlers connected to criminal and extremist networks overseas.
The reported surveillance has raised particular concern because of its similarities to the intelligence-gathering operations that preceded the November 2008 Mumbai terrorist attacks.
Months before those attacks, David Headley , a Pakistani-American operative working with the Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist organization, conducted extensive reconnaissance of potential targets in Mumbai, including the Chabad House. His surveillance helped the terrorists plan their deadly assault.
On November 26, 2008, terrorists launched coordinated attacks across Mumbai, killing 166 people over three days.
At the Chabad House, terrorists murdered Rabbi and Mrs. Holtzberg, along with four Jewish visitors. The Holtzbergs’ two-year-old son, Moshe , survived after his Indian nanny, Sandra Samuels , courageously rescued him from the building. He was subsequently brought to Israel.
The latest arrest comes less than two weeks before the 18th anniversary of the massacre.
In response to the reports, Chabad’s CWA Emergency and Security Center is calling on Shluchim around the world to increase their vigilance and review security precautions at their Chabad Houses.
“This report reminds us just how much vigilance can save lives,” the organization said.
The warning follows a security presentation at the International Kinus Hashluchim, where thousands of Shluchim watched a special video during Thursday night’s general session highlighting Chabad’s efforts to protect Shluchim and Chabad Houses around the world.
The presentation emphasized the importance of implementing security measures at Chabad institutions.
Indian authorities are continuing their investigation into Singh’s alleged connections with foreign networks. Investigators have not publicly established that the suspect was involved in planning a specific attack against the Chabad House.

articles.title_zh: IRS raises 401(k) contribution limit by $1,000 for 2027 as retirement savings caps increase
articles.content_orig:
The 2027 contribution limit for 401(k) plans is rising to $25,500, up $1,000 from 2026’s $24,500 cap.
The IRS has increased the amount workers can contribute to their 401(k) , up $1,000 from last year.
The government inflation-adjusted the 2027 limit to $25,500, a boost from 2026’s $24,500 limit, according to a recent IRS release.
"Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income," IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.
"With the new adjustment in place now, the IRS is giving taxpayers and employers the information needed to make retirement planning decisions for the year ahead."

The IRS has increased the amount workers can contribute to their 401(k), up $1,000 from last year. (Getty iStock / Getty Images)

For people 50 and over, the IRA catch-up contribution limit remains at $1,100. It was amended under the SECURE Act of 2022 to include an annual cost-of-living adjustment, according to the IRS.
The catch-up contribution limit for workers 50 and over with a 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans or the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan has gone up by $500 to $8,500.

The catch-up contribution limit that generally applies to employees aged 50 and over who participate in most 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans, and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan is increased to $8,500, up from $8,000 for 2026.
