articles.title_orig: Biden Reveals What Angela Merkel Really Thought of Donald Trump
articles.title_zh: Biden Reveals What Angela Merkel Really Thought of Donald Trump
articles.content_orig:
Former President Joe Biden has shared Angela Merkel 's private views of Donald Trump in his new White House memoir , revealing what the former German chancellor told him behind closed doors.
In excerpts shared with Newsweek from his forthcoming book, Promise Me, America , Biden recalls how Merkel candidly discussed her difficult relationship with Trump during their early conversations after he entered the White House in January 2021.
The former German chancellor described Trump as "emotional," and questioned his fascination with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other authoritarian leaders, Biden writes in the memoir.
Biden writes that Merkel was particularly frustrated by Trump's behavior during their meetings, including his refusal to shake her hand, and his apparent preference for personal impulses over established facts.
"In our conversations…Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts," Biden writes.
"She also wondered why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."
The revelations offer a glimpse into the private conversations Biden held with one of Europe's most influential leaders as he sought to rebuild relations with traditional American allies following four years of Trump's "America First" foreign policy.
Newsweek has reached out to Merkel and the White House for comment.
Merkel's relationship with Trump was frequently strained throughout his first presidency, with disagreements extending beyond their personal interactions to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's energy relationship with Russia.
One of their most memorable encounters came during Merkel's first Oval Office visit in March 2017.
Photographers captured an awkward moment when the two leaders sat alongside each other and were repeatedly encouraged to shake hands. Merkel turned toward Trump and quietly asked, "Do you want to have a handshake?"
Trump did not respond, remaining seated with his hands clasped as cameras continued taking photographs.
Merkel also reflected on the encounter in her 2024 memoir, Freedom , writing that she had initially approached Trump as though he were "someone completely normal." She described their interactions as feeling like "a competition: you or me."
Their disagreements also became increasingly public.
Trump repeatedly criticized Germany for failing to meet NATO's defense-spending target of 2 percent of gross domestic product, accusing Berlin of not contributing enough to the alliance and threatening to reconsider America's commitment to NATO.
He also threatened tariffs on German automotive exports and criticized Germany's support for the Nord Stream 2 natural gas pipeline, arguing that Berlin was making itself too dependent on Russian energy.
Merkel, meanwhile, opposed Trump's decisions to withdraw the United States from the 2015 Paris Climate Accord and the Iran nuclear deal.
Following a contentious G7 summit in Sicily in 2017, she warned that Europe could no longer completely rely on others.
"The times in which we could completely depend on others are, to a certain extent, over," Merkel said.
Her comments reflected growing concern among European leaders about the reliability of the trans-Atlantic relationship under Trump.
Biden's conversations with Merkel formed part of a broader effort to restore confidence among American allies when he took office in January 2021.
In Promise Me, America , he describes how he worked to reassure European leaders that Washington would once again engage with international institutions and traditional partners.
Merkel, who had served as German chancellor since 2005, ended her 16-year tenure in nDecember, 2021. During Trump's presidency, she had increasingly become a central figure in European discussions about the future of the Western alliance.
Biden writes that restoring those relationships was a priority, particularly as tensions with Russia continued to grow.
His account of Merkel's concerns about Putin is particularly notable given the developments that followed.
Biden reveals that U.S. intelligence agencies were increasingly concerning Russian military movements around Ukraine throughout 2021, months before Putin launched his full-scale invasion in February 2022.
He writes that he initially struggled to convince European allies, NATO members and Ukrainian officials that Putin was preparing to invade the entire country rather than pursue a more limited operation in the Donbas region.
The president eventually shared intelligence about Russian plans for a coup in Kyiv, including preparations for a propaganda video that he describes as an elaborate, almost "Hollywood production" designed to manufacture a pretext for an invasion.
Biden also recounts dispatching CIA Director Bill Burns to Moscow in November 2021 and personally confronting Putin in a phone call on December 7.
Merkel is among several international figures who feature prominently in Biden's retrospective of his presidency.
The memoir also contains candid accounts of his dealings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, whom Biden initially questioned whether he had the experience and resilience to withstand a full-scale military crisis.
Although Biden ultimately praised Zelensky's wartime leadership, he wrote they sometimes had a strained relationship, saying the Ukrainian leader could be "moody and stubborn" and "not as grateful as I would have expected" as he repeatedly pressed Washington for additional weapons and financial assistance.
Biden also revisits the chaotic August 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan in the book, writing that military and intelligence leaders had assured him the Afghan government and capital would remain standing for at least six months after American troops departed.
Instead, that assessment collapsed within days as Taliban forces advanced and Afghan President Ashraf Ghani fled the country.
The former president also reflects on meeting grieving families at Dover Air Force Base following the Abbey Gate bombing, which killed 13 American service members.
He acknowledges that some relatives viewed him as responsible for their suffering and that several would never forgive him.
Promise Me, America , published by Little, Brown and Company, is scheduled for release on Tuesday, November 17.

articles.title_orig: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.title_zh: How Jensen Huang Built the Backdoor Route That Keeps Beijing in the AI Race
articles.content_orig:
Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.
In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.
But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.
At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.
Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.
But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.
“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”
But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.
Nvidia’s CEO is out after 33 years. What’s next?
On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.
“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.
In another statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said that Huang left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there.
“Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” a statement seen by Reuters added.
In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.
US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.
Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.
Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.
“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.
In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.
Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.
“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.
“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.
Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.
In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.
The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.
A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.
Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.
However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.
They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”
Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.
Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.
Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: Fifth Canadian soldier dies of injuries from military training fire
articles.title_zh: Fifth Canadian soldier dies of injuries from military training fire
articles.content_orig:
EDMONTON, Alberta — A fifth Canadian soldier has died from injuries suffered when a wind-driven grass fire swept through troops during a military training exercise last month, the Canadian Armed Forces said Saturday.
Pvt. William Douglas Dal Bianco died Friday at a hospital in Ontario, where he had been receiving treatment since the Oct. 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the military said.
About 84 soldiers from the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were conducting attack training when winds pushed flames from a grass fire toward the troops at the base southeast of Edmonton.
The military said Saturday that 24 soldiers remain hospitalized.
“Private Dal Bianco and his fellow soldiers were training to defend Canada,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a social media post. “With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. That is service.”
The other soldiers killed were Pvt. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan; Pvt. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, British Columbia; Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, British Columbia; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.
Military police are investigating the fire, while a separate military board of inquiry will examine the circumstances of the tragedy and recommend measures to prevent similar incidents.
Carney has called the fire one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on Canadian soil.

articles.title_orig: US diesel below $6 a gallon at 2-month low on easing tensions, weaker demand
articles.title_zh: US diesel below $6 a gallon at 2-month low on easing tensions, weaker demand
articles.content_orig:
Oil markets have often reacted with strong downward moves whenever there has been a suggestion that all-out peace or at least an easing of Middle East tensions was at hand.
That has never been more true than in the days since the Democratic victories on Election Day. And it has now shown up in the benchmark diesel price used for most fuel surcharges.
The Department of Energy/Energy Information Administration’s average weekly retail price fell 16.5 cents/gallon to $6.127/g, effective Monday but published Tuesday.
It’s the second consecutive week of a decline, and it takes the price to its lowest level since October 12. That isn’t all that long ago, but neither is the highest price in the history of the series. That was recorded September 22, just seven weeks ago, when it reached $6.529/g.
The decline is coming as the futures market for ultra low sulfur diesel (ULSD) on the CME commodity exchange, and other oil contracts, are experiencing significant post-Election Day declines on the prospect of a Democratic Congress and a possibly chastened administration pulling back on more military action in the Middle East.
ULSD settled at $4.4216/g on the first day of the month. On Monday, it settled at $4.2148/g and at about 11:40 a.m. Tuesday, it was trading at $4.1409/g.
Brent, the world’s crude benchmark, settled at $104.77/barrel on the first trading day of November. It settled Monday at $92.57/b, and at 11:40 was at $91.55/b.
Amrita Sen, director of market intelligence at Energy Aspects, said in an interview Tuesday with Bloomberg Television that she believes the market has “erased it all” in regards to a risk premium as a result of the war.
She said trade data prior to the election suggested there was a significant amount of trade activity preparing for a post Election Day escalation of activity.
“People were positioning for an imminent strike,” Sen said. “When that didn’t happen, you definitely started to see the selloff.”
It’s been replaced, Sen said, by a market that is “now sanguine that the war will end no matter what from the U.S. side, because it’s not just the Democrats but also the Republicans don’t want the war to continue.”
The alternative more bullish view was expressed by the energy research team at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, which took the long view of where the oil market stands after months of lost output, damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia and flows through the Strait of Hormuz that are heavily dependent on U.S military support.
“Global oil supply disruptions have reached record levels in 2026, with the scale of the production shortfall exceeding anything seen in the historical data going back to 1965,” the team lead by Francisco Blanch wrote in a recent report. “The market entered the conflict unusually well supplied following several quarters of surplus, allowing inventories to absorb much of the initial disruption. But that cushion is being rapidly depleted, with particularly large stock draws in China and declining strategic inventories across OECD economies.”
The report reviews the hits to the world refining sector combined with inventory draws as resulting in a “market that has successfully absorbed an enormous physical shock so far, but with substantially less protection against the next one. Thus, the direction of the US-Iran war remains central to the evolution of oil prices over the next 12 months.”

articles.title_zh: Honda’s next CR-V raises a $4,510 question for buyers
articles.content_orig:
The current Honda CR-V can be had with or without a hybrid powertrain. However, when the compact SUV’s newest generation arrives sometime next year, it’ll only be available as a hybrid. Honda’s announcement comes a year after Toyota applied the same strategy with its new RAV4 . And considering over half the CR-Vs Honda sells are hybrids, the move makes a lot of sense.
Apart from introducing a standard hybrid powertrain, the 2028 Honda CR-V will mark the start of the bestselling nameplate’s seventh generation. It will also introduce a next-gen platform, which the automaker claims will prioritize stiffness and lightness; its modular nature will promote parts sharing too. While we’re still eagerly waiting for Honda to release more details about its next CR-V, the automaker has shared some breadcrumbs about its hybrid powertrain.
See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V for sale near 82001
The new fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid system will once again pair with an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder gas engine. We don’t yet know how much power the combo will make, but Honda says it “will greatly increase the standard power and efficiency.” When it comes to efficiency, the next-gen hybrid system is targeting an improvement of over 10 percent compared with the outgoing version. For reference, the current CR-V hybrid makes 205 horsepower, and it’s rated at up to 38 mpg combined.
We expect the 2028 Honda CR-V to be revealed sometime later this year. Honda says it’ll be the first of several hybrid models that it plans to launch by 2030.
Eric Stafford’s automobile addiction began before he could walk, and it has fueled his passion to write news, reviews, and more for Car and Driver since 2016. His aspiration growing up was to become a millionaire with a Jay Leno–like car collection. Apparently, getting rich is harder than social-media influencers make it seem, so he avoided financial success entirely to become an automotive journalist and drive new cars for a living. After earning a journalism degree at Central Michigan University and working at a daily newspaper, the years of basically burning money on failed project cars and lemon-flavored jalopies finally paid off when Car and Driver hired him. His garage currently includes a 2010 Acura RDX, a manual '97 Chevy Camaro Z/28, and a '90 Honda CRX Si.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Putin, Xi to Discuss Iran War at Unprecedented Trilateral Summit in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday, Nov. 19, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The Kremlin also confirmed the meeting on Saturday.
Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks and is also set to bring up the war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine , officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.
"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.
Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.
"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Mr. Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Mr. Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which then-U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain's Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations after World War II.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.
"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 14, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 14, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Increased cooperation among Yemeni government-aligned forces likely enabled these forces to successfully halt a Houthi offensive operation and recapture territory in southeastern Lahij Governorate. The Houthis launched a combined-arms offensive on November 11 that allowed Houthi fighters to advance approximately 12 kilometers southwest from al Majza into al Shatt and al Sarih Junction, both in Madaribah wa al Arah District, on November 12. [i] The southwest Houthi advance was part of a likely Houthi push toward Jabal Kharaz, which provides high ground from which the Houthis could threaten the Mokha-Aden ground line of communication and isolate Yemeni government-aligned forces operating on Yemen’s Red Sea coast. [ii]
Pervasive coordination and cooperation issues along southeastern frontlines may have enabled previous Houthi advances, such as the recent Houthi advance into al Shatt. The forces currently fighting for Yemen’s internationally recognized government consist of a variety of factions with varying objectives and command structures that hamper coordination and cooperation among the fighters, particularly in southeastern Yemen, although this issue persists across the various fronts. [iii] One of the more influential factions within this coalition is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a political organization that controls some forces in the south and seeks to form independent southern Yemeni state. STC-backed military forces in southern Yemen fight for the Yemeni government but often compete with other government-aligned forces. Some STC-backed groups reportedly refused to allow the northern Yemeni government-aligned forces withdrawing from Yemen’s Red Sea coastal plain to enter Aden City in early September, for example. [iv] At least some STC-backed groups have more recently refused to operate outside the former borders of the Democratic People’s Republic of Yemen, which includes Lahij and Aden governorates, until the Yemeni government grants the Yemeni people a referendum on southern Yemeni secession. [v]
The threat that the Houthi advance poses to southern Yemeni territory likely motivated some STC-backed groups to coordinate with the forces currently fighting against the Houthi forces in southwestern Lahij Governorate. The Support and Reinforcement Brigades, an STC-aligned faction, began to reinforce the Southern Giants Brigades and Homeland Shield Forces in southwest Lahij Governorate on November 12. [vi] This marks the first time the Support and Reinforcement Brigades have deployed to the Madaribah wa al Arah front since the start of the campaign, according to an independent Yemeni journalist. [vii] The Support and Reinforcement Brigades likely decided to deploy and coordinate with the Southern Giants Brigades and Homeland Shield Forces because the Houthi advances on November 12 threatened to consolidate Houthi control over territory in southern Lahij Governorate, which is territory that is part of the independent southern Yemeni state that these groups seek to form. Many Support and Reinforcement Brigades fighters, including senior commanders, are from southern Lahij Governorate and are members of local Lahij-based tribes. [viii] The involvement of the Support and Reinforcement Brigades likely contributed to the successful counterattack in which government forces recaptured both al Shatt and al Sarih on November 13. [ix] Yemeni government-aligned forces also reportedly continued to advance and engaged Houthi fighters near al Majza later on November 13. [x]
The Yemeni government is attempting to improve coordination among Yemeni government-aligned groups by establishing a unified command structure for units operating in southwestern Yemen. A Yemeni military source said on November 12 that the Yemeni government implemented a unified joint command structure for forces currently operating in Lahij Governorate, including the Southern Giants Brigades, Homeland Shield Forces, and Support and Reinforcement Brigades, and other local groups. [xi] Another independent Yemeni journalist reported on November 13 that the Yemeni government has appointed former Homeland Shield Forces Commander Bashir al Mazarbi al Shuaihi to lead the unified forces. [xii] The Yemeni government has not announced Shuaihi’s appointment at the time of this writing.
Saudi aircraft simultaneously provided close air support to aid the Yemeni government-aligned forces’ counterattack by targeting Houthi frontline units in Madaribah wa al Arah District and Houthi logistics necessary to sustain Houthi operations in the area. Saudi aircraft targeted Houthi forces and materiel in al Turbah, southern Taiz Governorate, a key staging area for the Houthis that is located about 30 kilometers north of al Majza. [xiii] Saudi aircraft reportedly targeted Houthi supply lines in al Maqatirah and al Shamayatayn districts which are also located north of al Majza and likely supported Houthi operations around al Shatt and al Sarih. [xiv] Saudi aircraft also targeted Houthi forces and vehicles on the frontline as Yemeni government-aligned forces, including the Southern Giants and Homeland Shield Forces, launched counterattacks against the Houthis in unspecified locations within Madaribah wa al Arah District on November 13. [xv]
The Iraqi federal government began a highly circumscribed investigation into Kataib Hezbollah's involvement in oil smuggling in Jurf al Sakhr, Babil Province, on November 13. An Iraqi federal government investigation committee conducted a field inspection of Kataib Hezbollah's Jurf al Sakhr stronghold on November 13, according to multiple Iraqi media reports and footage from the area. [xvi] Kataib Hezbollah has not allowed federal authorities to enter Jurf al Sakhr in over a decade. [xvii] The government visit follows a recent leaked, "top-secret" Iraqi Interior Ministry report that revealed how Kataib Hezbollah has generated millions of dollars in illicit revenue from oil smuggling in the Jurf al Sakhr area since 2021. [xviii] Zaydi directed on November 13 the formation of a Jurf al Sakhr investigation committee chaired by the Kataib Hezbollah-affiliated head of the Popular Mobilization Commission's Security and Discipline Directorate and consisting of other federal government representatives. [xix] The Popular Mobilization Commission is the Popular Mobilization Forces' administrative body. [xx] Iraqi media reported that the investigation committee and a contingent of Iraqi Federal Police met with Iraqi militia members—almost certainly from Kataib Hezbollah—before the inspection. [xxi] The committee reportedly agreed with the militia members on the investigation’s mechanisms and the "arrangement of the committee's rounds," which probably refers to how and where the committee would investigate oil smuggling in Jurf al Sakhr. [xxii]
Zaydi almost certainly made a deal with Iranian-backed Iraqi actors to allow an investigation of this nature as a balance between efforts to hold Iranian-backed Iraqi militias accountable and efforts to avoid armed conflict with Kataib Hezbollah. This investigation, which appears to be highly coordinated with the militias, follows a previous attempt by the government to enter Jurf al Sakhr without militia permission. Iraqi media reported that Iraqi Army, Federal Police, and Counter Terrorism Service units prepared on November 12 to escort an Iraqi government investigative committee into Jurf al Sakhr to inspect smuggling-related oil storage sites, tankers, and transport routes. articles.title_orig: Omaha pizza place closes both its Blackstone and Aksarben locations
articles.title_zh: Omaha pizza place closes both its Blackstone and Aksarben locations
articles.content_orig:
OMAHA, Neb. — Noli's Pizzeria is shuttering its two locations after nearly 12 years in business, the restaurant announced in a social media post Saturday evening
In the post, Noli's said its fans were the reason it survived, and the restaurant pledged to take care of its employees as it closes.
"We're closed, though. Appreciate you. You are the reason we were here for near 12 years. Love you all," the restaurant wrote. The post went on to invite the community to celebrate the restaurant's memory with a New Orleans-style send-off, adding, "Celebrate and remember the heart. That will never leave. Love."
The restaurant also made clear its staff would be a priority. "And we are going to take care of our employees. Never a question on that," the post said.
The closure comes just weeks after a major setback. The location near 40th and Farnam, in Omaha's Blackstone neighborhood, temporarily closed in September after two of its coolers failed within six weeks, and owner Joel Marsh said at the time that he did not have the money to replace them. A GoFundMe campaign raised more than $10,000 following that setback.
Despite that community support, both locations are now closing permanently.
The struggles had been building for years. Marsh has said streetcar construction in the Blackstone neighborhood hurt the business over the past two years, with the location seeing more than $300,000 in lost revenue.
"For nine years, Noli's Blackstone has been a small business my family and I have been incredibly proud of. Over the last two years, streetcar construction has changed everything. Sales have fallen substantially while food, labor, and operating costs have continued to rise, and we have been struggling just to keep our employees paid and the doors open," Marsh said in the GoFundMe.
RELATED: Noli's Pizzeria overwhelmed by community support after social media plea
Through those struggles, the community repeatedly rallied around the restaurant. In January, after Marsh posted on Facebook about the toll of construction and winter weather, neighbors sold out more than $25,000 in gift cards in two days.
"It was overwhelming and a very humbling experience. The community came out and we sold over $25,000 in gift cards in two days, which is, I can't even believe it," Marsh said at the time.
Noli's has long been a fixture in the Blackstone neighborhood. The restaurant donated thousands of dollars in meals to neighbors facing food insecurity, including giveaways during the government shutdown last year.
For Marsh, the restaurant was always more than a business.
"I built all of these, like with my dad, bare hands, all these tables, every surface. At the other restaurant and here, we built. I mean every recipe, everything you see is art to me," Marsh said earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Howard Lutnick in the hot seat as lawmakers demand answers on Nvidia sales to China
articles.title_zh: Howard Lutnick in the hot seat as lawmakers demand answers on Nvidia sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Howard Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology to Asia, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales in the region. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times
By Ana Swanson Tripp Mickle Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
Ana Swanson, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported from Washington, and Tripp Mickle from San Francisco.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang , was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company , sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Carried a Secret for More Than a Year. It Led to His Downfall.
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang was one of the world's most influential figures in the tech and AI industry. ( Reuters: Mike Blake )
Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO.
The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs.
While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain.
China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". ( Reuters: CTI )
When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month.
Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address.
Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2.
Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances.
"There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter.
Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees.
His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with.
In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security".
Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders .
Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China.
In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development.
That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology.
Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. ( Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz )
Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist.
In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list.
The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade.
Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China.
Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well.
The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment.
In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him.
He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May.
The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year.
The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.
When asked in recent days whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, Mr Trump said "I don't think so" and maintained that Mr Huang was an "honourable guy".
The president has continued to stand by Mr Huang and said the tech billionaire told him he had no idea Ms Huang was a spy, and that he believed him.
On the day Mr Huang admitted to his affair, Nvidia announced it had called an independent investigation into whether their then-chief executive had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort".
But early in the piece, the company said it had "no reason to believe" either US national security or company secrets had been compromised.
There was no mention of the investigation when Nvidia announced its current executive vice-president and chief financial officer Colette Kress was stepping in as interim CEO.
Instead, Nvidia's new chair Harvey C Jones said: "We expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."
It remains to be seen as to whether the investigation finds evidence Mr Huang gave away sensitive information — or whether its findings are publicly revealed.
Ms Huang, who's been identified as a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, has not commented publicly since the Nvidia scandal erupted.
China has denied she is a spy and US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was or not.
Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports.
Singaporean authorities also said they questioned Ms Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed's exports.
They concluded there wasn't enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed.
Ms Huang left Singapore in February when she received her passport back and was banned from re-entering the country.
She is currently living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The Singapore home affairs ministry said investigations into Megaspeed and six individuals were ongoing.
Megaspeed said on Thursday it took compliance obligations under US export control laws "extremely seriously", adding it had cooperated with US inspections.

articles.content_orig:
Hamas has confirmed that Rafah brigade commander Samir Abu Younis was killed in an Israeli air strike on the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, southern Gaza.
Israel’s military and Shin Bet security agency earlier said in a joint statement that they had targeted a senior Hamas military commander in a drone strike in Khan Younis on Saturday.
Early on Sunday, hours after the attack, Hamas said in a statement that the person targeted was a senior member of its military wing.
Saturday’s strike that hit a tent sheltering displaced people wounded two others.
The casualties were taken to Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis, medical personnel told Al Jazeera on Saturday.
Video footage verified by Al Jazeera and posted by Palestinian journalists from the vicinity of the hospital showed ambulances inside the grounds and stretchers that appear to be stained with blood.
Al-Mawasi, a coastal strip on the Mediterranean, is crowded with displaced Palestinians living in tents. Israel has repeatedly attacked the area despite previously designating it a humanitarian zone.
Gaza’s Ministry of Health said in its latest update on Saturday that Israeli attacks have killed 16 people and injured 68 others over the past 48 hours.
Since the “ceasefire” in Gaza took effect on October 11, 2025, Israel has killed at least 1,643 Palestinians and injured 5,964. At least 850 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.
Since Israel began its genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, at least 74,695 people have been killed and 176,093 injured, according to the Health Ministry.
The ministry also reported that the number of deaths related to cold has risen to 11 after a nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia, the first this winter.
Gaza’s residents, most of whom have been displaced, are living in tents and damaged buildings as water damage from recent heavy rains has set in.
Israeli attacks have escalated across Gaza, despite the October ceasefire.

articles.title_orig: Iran's fuel rationing system reaches breaking point with hours-long lines, protests on eve of ‘Bloody November’
articles.title_zh: Iran's fuel rationing system reaches breaking point with hours-long lines, protests on eve of ‘Bloody November’
articles.content_orig:
Motorists across Iran were trapped in grueling hours-long lines at gas stations and taxi drivers took to the streets in protest Saturday, as the state’s fuel rationing system reached a breaking point — hours before the infamous anniversary of “Bloody November.”
In one video shared on Telegram, drivers at a gas station in the southern city of Kazeroun are heard shouting in anger about the fuel shortages.
“To the officials: don’t mess with Kazeroun. This city has shown many times that it does not remain silent in the face of neglect and ignoring the demands of the people,” one Iranian Telegram account commented Saturday.
A video sent to Iran International by a local resident shows long lines of vehicles waiting to refuel at night in Evaz, a city in southern Iran's Fars province, amid fuel shortages and rising prices. pic.twitter.com/cEf9Y1ucia
“These days, long queues at gas stations in Kazeroun have become one of the main concerns of the people.”
In other videos, lines of cars can be seen stretching for miles in southern Iranian cities that include Kazeroun, Bandar Abbas, Evaz and Lordegan.
In Ardabil in the north, footage shows taxi drivers parking their cars in protest, leaving passengers stranded as they refuse to pick them up.
Sunday marks seven years since Iran was rocked by “Bloody November.”
Just after midnight on Nov. 15, 2019, Iran announced a dramatic price hike — from 10,000 to 15,000 rials per liter for the first 60 liters of gas a month, then 30,000 rials after that — an increase of 50% and 300%, respectively, overnight.
Within hours, nationwide protests sparked, with Iranians blocking highways with their cars, burning banks and tearing down images of then Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
After a day of unrest, the iron-fisted Ayatollah told senior commanders to “do whatever it takes to end it,” resulting in one of the deadliest crackdowns in the Islamic Republic’s hardline history.
An estimated 1,500 Iranians were slaughtered over the course of less than two weeks.
Fearing a possible repeat, the government has avoided another price hike since, instead rationing gasoline to 160 liters a month per vehicle.
But a collapsing economy, due to Washington’s crippling sanctions, government corruption and now the  US blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, has deeply worsened shortages and put tensions inside Iran on the brink.
Until last month, Iranians could fill up with a gas station’s own “emergency card” after they ran out of their monthly ration, at a higher price of 100,000 rials. That accounted for nearly half the gasoline sold across the country.
But since Nov. 1, the regime has taken away emergency cards in more than a third of Iran, with plans to strip the rest within weeks.
A state official even admitted this week, “we really have a supply problem” — in comments that have raised the ire of the government, Iran International reported.
“All the gasoline the government has, it has given to the people,” said Esmail Sagheb Esfahani, vice president of the State Energy Efficiency Agency. “Nothing has been held back to supply more.”

articles.title_orig: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.title_zh: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.content_orig:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".
Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.
The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.
It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.
Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.
So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.
He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.
It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.
The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.
Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.
He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".
In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".
He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its Starship rocket as it returned to Earth
Using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower, the top part of the rocket was captured intact
SpaceX referred to the success as "picture perfect"

Wedaeli Chibelushi Live reporter
Elon Musk's SpaceX has successfully caught the top part of its Starship rocket during its descent back down to Earth - a key milestone for the company.
It's the first time SpaceX captured a detachable section of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
SpaceX's spokesman described the feat, which took concluded in Texas, as the "Holy Grail of space flight". "Now everything changes," he added.
We're now ending our live coverage, but you can watch the moment of the successful capture in the video below:
Huge cheers were heard as the "Ship" of Starship landed safely in the mechanical arms of the launchpad.
In the background, Baby Come Back by Player was heard over the video feed.
"That was the Holy Grail of space flight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship and now everything changes," AFP quotes SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot as saying.
The top part of the rocket, known as the Ship, was caught by the mechanical arms of the launch tower
SpaceX has successfully caught part of the Starship rocket.
It was captured as it returned to Earth intact by mechanical arms, known as chopsticks, on the launch tower.
SpaceX is hoping to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth - you can watch the attempt live above.
The company is aiming to capture the rocket booster using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
The first attempt was unsuccessful and was aborted. The booster was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The booster of the SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 explodes after the first failed attempt
The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday - but this is subject to change.
This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket.

articles.title_zh: A new 'Yalta'? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Donald Trump will meet Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China next week for an unprecedented three-way meeting between the leaders of the US , Russia , and China, with nuclear weapons and the war in Iran expected to be on the agenda.
The meeting will take place on Thursday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, the White House confirmed on Friday. It will bring together the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers for the first time, although all three have held bilateral talks with one another.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
The meeting comes nine months after the expiry of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), the last major nuclear arms control agreement between Washington and Moscow.
The treaty, which expired in February, had placed limits on the two countries’ strategic nuclear arsenals, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without those restrictions for the first time in more than half a century.
Mr Trump has rejected Russia's offer to extend it for another year, saying he wanted a new agreement that would also include China.
Beijing has resisted joining such negotiations, arguing that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Washington and Moscow. China has more than 600 nuclear warheads, compared with more than 5,000 each for Russia and the US.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told reporters, according to Reuters. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think ​it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have ​adult conversations about adult things.”
Mr Trump also intends to discuss the war in Iran with Mr Xi and Mr Putin, but Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is not expected to feature, the official said. “We’ve had many meetings ⁠recently with ​the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, ​so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the official said.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that his country must be involved in any discussions about its future.
Russia had previously proposed the three-way meeting, with Mr Putin reportedly keen to use it to discuss Ukraine. The Russian president had floated the idea during a telephone conversation with Trump last month, according to the Wall Street Journal .
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha had warned against giving Putin such a platform. “Inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandisement and give him a stature he does not deserve,” he said last month, adding that it would only “encourage Putin to continue this war”.
The planned summit has also drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union discussed the postwar settlement in Europe. The prospect of Mr Trump, Mr Putin, and Mr Xi meeting without Ukraine has revived concerns about major powers making decisions that affect other countries without consulting them.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the comparison, saying that any agreements reached in Shenzhen could not be imposed on other countries. He nevertheless described a meeting between the three leaders as “extremely significant”. “However, let’s not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect,” he said.
Mr Trump is due to visit Manila on Tuesday for talks with leaders of the Association of South-east Asian Nations before heading to Shenzhen. He is also scheduled to hold bilateral talks and a working lunch with Xi on Thursday, ahead of the trilateral meeting.
The White House said billionaire Elon Musk would accompany Mr Trump on the China visit, but a senior US official said he would not attend the talks with Mr Xi and Mr Putin.

articles.title_orig: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.title_zh: US aviation shutdown blamed on L3 Harris installed router
articles.content_orig:
Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they recovered from Friday's nationwide ground stop, but the FAA said schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
More than 5,000 U.S. flights had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware , already past the top of the 4,000 to 5,000 that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted. Flight-tracking app Flighty said the outage has now caused more cancellations than the 2024 CrowdStrike software failure. "I do think the worst is behind us," Bedford said, and he apologized to travelers.
The FAA halted departures nationwide for more than four hours Friday, the longest ground stop since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks. About 12,000 flights couldn't be completed, Bedford said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage began while L3Harris Technologies, which runs the network, was doing routine work to switch lines from copper wire to fiber at a remote FAA site. A router involved in the work flooded the rest of the system, disrupting communications with airplanes and radar. Duffy said officials are working to determine "whether we had incompetence" by the contractor or a faulty router. "Until I can build" a new network, he said, "I'm stuck with L3Harris." Bedford said the review will determine whether the router was installed or configured incorrectly, or was simply defective.
In a statement to Yahoo News, L3Harris said it is "supporting the FAA in its investigation" and "takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." The company did not address Duffy's criticism or say what went wrong.
Asked why the work was done on a Friday afternoon, Duffy said work at small, remote sites is done during the day because it isn't expected to affect the wider system. "There'll be a reevaluation of when we do this work," he said. Bedford said maintenance on the network is logged on paper, so officials had to search through paper records to figure out who was working where.
Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told Yahoo News that communications with some planes were disrupted during the outage and that controllers moved flights to working frequencies. Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, he said, "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky."
The network's problems aren't new. A 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review called it obsolete, CBS News reported . In 2009, a technician for L3Harris' predecessor, Harris Corp., misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 air traffic facilities, according to a Transportation Department inspector general review .
Duffy is pressing Congress for more money to replace the system. President Trump has asked for $30 billion and Duffy has said he wants $50 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. Bedford said the router swap was routine maintenance, not part of that modernization effort.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign Saturday. Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation .
Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and most major airlines are offering travel waivers. Airlines' promises of hotels and meals generally cover only disruptions within their control, which doesn't include an FAA ground stop.
National Air Traffic Controllers Association President Nick Daniels speaks during a news conference at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on September 28, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The head of the air traffic controllers' union told Yahoo News in a phone interview Saturday that communications with some planes were disrupted during Friday's outage. Controllers across the country had to scramble to keep flights moving safely, he said.
"We had controllers working with one another across the United States to see whose frequencies were working, whose radar was working," said Nick Daniels, president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association. Controllers checked whether they could hand off planes to one another if their own frequencies went down, he said.
Daniels said he hadn't reviewed the FAA's safety data. But asked what controllers had told him, he said, "We know we didn't have communications with airplanes, or that we were switching airplanes to different frequencies because their communications were being disrupted." Controllers "ensured the safety of every aircraft," he said.
FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a news conference earlier Saturday that "no facilities went dark," but acknowledged reports of "certain frequencies that were going in and out."
Asked whether work like Friday's should be done during the day, Daniels said it depends on the risk. "If the worst outcome is we lose all of our frequencies, well, then that work should be done when there's the fewest airplanes in the sky," he said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that work at small, remote sites is routinely done during the day and that the practice will be reevaluated.
Daniels said such failures often happen when the FAA's required safety reviews before maintenance aren't followed. He said he didn't know whether that happened Friday.
Daniels wouldn't say whether Duffy was right to blame contractor L3Harris. "I don't think blame changes anything. Action changes things," Daniels said. He said the union has warned for more than a decade that the system is failing, noting that the FAA still uses floppy disks in some cases to update computers.
Daniels said any new money for the air traffic control system should also go toward controllers' pay and working conditions. He said he hasn't spoken with Duffy since the outage, but that Duffy "already knows" the union's position. "We're going to continue working on that with this administration," he said.
More than 5,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday as of 2:48 p.m. ET, according to FlightAware . FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had predicted 4,000 to 5,000 cancellations for the day.
American has canceled the most flights, 892, followed by Delta (734), United (733) and Southwest (540). JetBlue has canceled 43% of its schedule.
The air traffic control system itself appears to be running near normal, and no airports had ground stops in effect Saturday afternoon. The problem now is getting planes and crews back where they're supposed to be.
Sunday looks better so far. About 130 U.S. flights scheduled for Sunday had been canceled as of Saturday afternoon.
L3Harris Technologies said Saturday it is supporting the FAA's investigation into Friday's outage. Earlier that day, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly questioned whether the company's "incompetence" caused the outage.
"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," an L3Harris spokesperson said in a statement to Yahoo News. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
The company said that, "together with its telco partners and the FAA," it has completed more than 70% of the planned switch from copper wire to fiber optic lines. The statement doesn't say what caused the outage or respond to Duffy's suggestion of contractor error.
Asked whether L3Harris employees or a partner company did Friday's work, and whether the company disputes Duffy's suggestion of contractor error, a spokesperson said the company had nothing to offer beyond its statement.
Airlines' biggest challenge Saturday is getting pilots and flight attendants to the planes they're scheduled to fly.

articles.title_orig: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.title_zh: What Travelers Caught in the Air-Travel Delays Need to Know
articles.content_orig:
"The airlines are trying to get back to normal."
As air travel in the United States remains hectic due to the lingering effects from Friday's ground stop , a travel expert said preparation and patience are key for flyers who are trying to reach their destination.
Brett Snyder, the president of the travel planning service Cranky Concierge, said that flight schedules will likely not be back to normal until Monday at the earliest as airlines scramble to get their fleets and crews back to their planned destinations as orderly as possible.
A total of over 14,000 flights were canceled Friday and Saturday, according to FlightAware. Around 160 flights on Sunday have been canceled as of Saturday afternoon, FlightAware said.
The FAA said the ground stop was instituted due to a telecommunications issue in the air traffic control system.
FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the system is expected to be fully recovered by Sunday.
"The point of the cancellations and delays today is to right the ship as quick as possible and by Monday everything is as smooth as possible," Snyder told ABC News Saturday.
Snyder said that while there's not a lot passengers can do while the airlines and airports recover, there are key steps they can take to help ensure their flights go as smooth as possible.
The first thing that flyers should consider is if it's worth waiting for their flight if it has been delayed or if they should rebook, he said.
"If this was a trip that was going to be short and fun and not a big deal, I'd scrap it," Snyder said.
Snyder said that most airlines are offering refunds during this situation, even if their planned flight is delayed.
American Airlines announced Saturday it is adding fare caps across their domestic and short international flights as delays are expected to continue. American, Southwest, Delta and United are all offering travelers waivers.
Travelers are entitled to refunds for flights canceled by the airlines, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation.
"The consumer is entitled to a refund if the airline cancelled a flight, regardless of the reason, and the consumer chooses not to travel or accept travel credits, vouchers, or other forms of compensation offered by the airline," DOT says on its website .
Additionally, travelers are entitled to a refund if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and they choose not to accept credits, vouchers or other compensation offered by the airline.
DOT defines a significantly delayed flight as three or more hours after the original scheduled arrival time for domestic flights.
For those who are still pushing ahead with their trip, Snyder said it's best to stay at the airport and remain on top of any updates. He recommended travelers download the airline's app and keeping an eye on all the alerts associated with their flight.
Snyder noted that flyers should pay close attention to any connecting flights and check if they are canceled. Airlines are typically good at rebooking customers during those situations, he added.
When in doubt, Snyder recommended that flyers call their airlines. If they are in the airport, talk to an agent, he said.
He stressed that ticket holders should remain courteous to the representatives.
"Remember the airline employees are going through this just as much you are as a traveler. Go easy on them, they're trying to help you," Snyder said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Saturday that the federal government is working around the clock to help the airlines and airports navigate through the issues and get service back to normal as fast as possible.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most," Duffy said in a post on X earlier Saturday.
"Our top priority right now is making sure travelers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible," Duffy said.
