articles.title_orig: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.title_zh: FAA ground stop lifted: NYC-airports facing delays, cancellations after communication issue
articles.content_orig:
The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop just after 8 p.m. on Friday
NEW YORK (WABC) -- Thousands of travelers across the New York area are grappling with the effects of a nationwide ground stop, with nearly 2,000 flights canceled across the country on Saturday.
The disruptions are being felt across the region at Newark Liberty International Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport, and LaGuardia Airport, as passengers face delays, cancellations, and uncertain travel plans. Officials are hoping operations return to normal before the busy Thanksgiving travel period begins.
Port Authority released a statement Saturday saying,
"Travelers should anticipate continued delays and cancellations at the region's airports throughout the weekend as airlines recover from Friday night's nationwide FAA ground stop. By the end of Friday evening, JFK, LaGuardia, and New York Stewart airports had reported more than 800 cancellations and more than 600 delays.
Airlines are continuing to work through the logistical challenges created by Friday's disruption. Planes were left out of position across the country, and some flight attendants reached their allowable duty limits, requiring carriers to reassign crews and equipment before flights can return to normal schedules.
15% of flights were canceled out of Newark Saturday, 21% at LaGuardia, and 21% at JFK Airport. There were dozens of delays at all three airports.
On Friday evening at LaGuardia, one of the nation's busiest transportation hubs, only a handful of international flights were arriving after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights to stop departing.
Video from the airport around 4:30 p.m. showed aircraft on the runway. About 30 minutes later, roughly a dozen planes were stopped in place as pilots received instructions to return to their gates.
"Nobody is allowed to leave the ground. If you are on the ground, please return to the gate immediately," pilots were told.
Even after flights resumed, some travelers remained stranded or scrambling to adjust their plans.
One passenger trying to reach Belize said the disruption left him frustrated after he missed his flight.
"Unfortunately, we did not make over our flight ... hopefully make it home," he said.
The FAA said it issued the nationwide ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."
Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said at a press conference Saturday.
"We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI-related. So we want to be clear that we have a equipment issue, and we're working through what this defective piece of equipment was," Bedford said.
"When we have that root cause analysis complete, we'll share it with you," Bedford said.
He predicted the air travel schedule would fully recover by Sunday.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA does not believe the failure in communications that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday was the result of a cyber attack.
"In at least one of our remote FAA locations, a contractor was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from old copper wire, and they were bringing it over to fiber," Duffy said during a press conference Saturday.
Duffy said this transfer from copper to fiber has been happening in the U.S. for decades, saying virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital.
"Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system. So specifically, we had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was gave us issues with our our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar feeds," Duffy said.
When that happened the airspace was shut down for safety, Duffy said.
"Once we were able to isolate the work that was being done at this remote location, all of our systems came back online, so we don't believe this was cyber at all. This was an FAA system that didn't meet, didn't meet the moment," Duffy said.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul released a statement saying: "America's airspace ground to a halt yesterday, leaving thousands of flights canceled and travelers stranded across the country. More than 3,500 planes were already in the air as radar and communications systems faltered. We're fortunate no lives were lost.
"From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy's watch.
"Through it all, he's been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency.
"With millions of Americans preparing to travel for the holidays, families deserve answers and confidence in the safety of our skies. Congress must launch a full investigation to determine what went wrong and ensure it never happens again.
"Sean Duffy must resign, or President Trump must remove him immediately."
Major airlines have issued travel waivers for affected passengers this weekend.
American Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines are waiving change fees through Saturday, with United also waiving fare differences. Southwest Airlines is allowing passengers to rebook at no additional cost through Monday.
Travelers are encouraged to check directly with their airline and review the status of their itinerary before heading to the airport as carriers continue working to minimize delays and cancellations.
The disruption marked the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned.
Before that, the last nationwide ground stop occurred after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.title_zh: Nvidia board urged to consider 'potential return of Jensen Huang' by two major investors
articles.content_orig:
Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.
Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday amid multiple affair allegations, including one with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang , who also worked with Nvidia customer Megaspeed . The Singapore-based company is being investigated by the Justice Department for possibly redirecting some of its supply of Nvidia's restricted artificial intelligence chips to China.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on X Friday that he signed a petition asking to reinstate Huang. A petition circulating online called "Stand with Jensen" claims to have more than 100,000 signatures, including more than 5,000 current Nvidia employees.
Musk said on X Saturday that without Huang, some "critical deals will be lost."
Another letter sent Friday called on U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee.
Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 about whether the Commerce Department is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips," according to the letter. Huang has also been asked to testify .
The Commerce Department originally launched an investigation into Megaspeed that was moved to the Justice Department in 2025 after Nvidia's lawyer contacted a senior Commerce official, according to The New York Times.
President Donald Trump is scheduled to visit China on Thursday, but doesn't plan to raise Nvidia and the suspected spy affair during his meeting with Chinese president Xi Jinping , according to U.S. officials. Musk is expected to join Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.

articles.title_orig: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
articles.title_zh: Pope laments violence enveloping Peru as he ministers in his former diocese
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has called for an end to the violence gripping Peru, urging people not to respond to injustice with brutality, as he visited communities he once served as bishop.
“We feel threatened by the uncertainty of widespread violence and by the unspeakable suffering that continues to afflict so many of our brothers and sisters, he said, speaking at his former cathedral in Chiclayo.
Peru’s homicide rate has nearly doubled over the past five years, from 5.8 to 10.7 per 100,000 people. Reported extortion cases rose from 2,421 in 2019 to 26,734 in 2025, according to official figures cited by The Associated Press.
Security was a top concern for Peruvians in the last election. Conservative President Keiko Fujimori took office in July after promising to tackle crime. She has since declared states of emergency, including in Lima in August, then in September in prisons holding inmates linked to criminal organisations.
She has also pursued closer ties with Washington, bringing Peru into the ‘Shield of the Americas,’ a US-led regional coalition formed to carry out joint military operations against drug cartels.
Later on Saturday, in the Andean town of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba with a population of about 6,000, about 20,000 people came to an outdoor Mass, where Leo also addressed violence in society.
“Selfishness, injustice and evil are not overcome by brutality, but by prayer, patience and perseverance in denouncing what is wrong, by making our pleas with determination and working diligently to bring about the necessary changes,” said the leader of the Roman Catholic church.
He also drew attention to the suffering of rural communities he used to serve, where migration and declining birth rates are emptying villages.
“Let us think, for example, of the suffering of those who are forced to leave their homeland in search of a better future for themselves and their families in the great coastal cities,” he said.
Originally from Chicago in the United States and formerly known as Robert Francis Prevost, Leo arrived in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba by helicopter and was welcomed by a local band singing “Pope Leo, welcome home.”
He’d made the journey to the remote area many times before during his time as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, driving himself along winding mountain roads in a pick-up truck.
The pope, who holds both US and Peruvian citizenship, spent about two decades working in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented joint meeting on APEC sidelines, White House and Kremlin say
articles.content_orig:
The leaders of the US, Russia and China will meet late next week, according to the White House
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China , which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

articles.title_orig: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
articles.content_orig:
By OLIVIA CHRISTIE, NEWS REPORTER
Published: 10:06 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 12:49 EST, 14 November 2026
Andy Burnham claimed today that Britain has ‘lost more than we gained’ in the decade since the Brexit referendum – as he pressed ahead with his push for closer ties with Brussels.
Ahead of meeting European leaders at a UK-EU summit next week, the Prime Minister said a new deal he hopes to secure will ‘get food prices down’ and put more money in the pockets of British exporters.
Mr Burnham is expected to sign new agreements on food, emissions trading and youth mobility – arguing that he could strike a ‘win-win’ deal that could increase GDP by 0.4 per cent. He has said he will then ‘explore options’ for a different long-term relationship with the trading bloc.
But critics say the ‘reset’ could cost the UK £750million a week in membership fees and force us to adopt a new EU regulation every 12 hours.
Speaking at Welsh Labour conference today, the PM said: ‘We need to be willing to take difficult decisions to get the cost of living down.
‘It’s why, in a few days’ time, I will head to the next UK-EU summit and I will be working hard as we move towards it to get to a new deal on food and farming between the UK and the EU.
‘Why am I doing that? Because I want to help Welsh businesses.
‘I want to remove some of the red tape that food exporters here face when they are seeking to send their product support abroad, but more than anything I’m trying to get prices down, food prices down, and if we get the right deal, that is what we will do, as well as reduce costs for businesses, and overall get more growth into the UK economy, up to 0.4 per cent on GDP.’
Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaking during the Welsh Labour conference today
He added: 'Why wouldn't I do that as Prime Minister? Why wouldn't I lead in that way? We've got the Conservatives who are standing out against it, saying no change. Well, I don't believe Brexit and the deal that they got has been good enough for Britain.
'I think we've lost more than we've gained over the last 10 years, and, actually, I think the Conservatives gave Britain a harsher and harder Brexit than people thought they were getting when they voted in 2016, because they burned all of our bridges in the aftermath, with the EU, and so I'm going to lead as Prime Minister on this issue, and I'm going to go and try and get the best deal I can for Wales, for those here who could benefit, Welsh farmers, exporters of Welsh shellfish and Welsh lamb.'
His comments come after a new campaign group claimed that the bill for Britain to re-join the EU would be a staggering £750million a week .
The group, Stay Out, blames Brussels' spiralling budget, a doubling of its borrowing costs and no chance of recovering the UK's special rebate negotiated by former prime minister Margaret Thatcher.
The cost warning has echoes of Vote Leave's controversial campaign bus slogan, suggesting £350million per week could be clawed back from the EU and spent on the NHS. The Stay Out study reveals that the size of the EU’s annual budget has doubled since then and could land us with annual payments of £39.3billion a year.
Deputy Conservative leader Alex Burghart said Mr Burnham's focus on the future of the UK-EU relationship was a tactic to distract from rising welfare costs and questions about defence funding.
'Nearly a decade after the Brexit referendum, Andy Burnham is reopening a debate the country settled long ago, while ignoring the challenges facing Britain today,' he said.
'Instead of tackling the spiralling welfare bill, fixing our economy and properly funding our defence, Burnham is preparing to hand Brussels more money in an effort to distract from the mess his party has gotten us into.
'British taxpayers deserve to know why money is being committed to projects across Europe when this Government claims it cannot afford to address priorities at home. A Conservative government would work to take this country forwards, not backwards.'
The Prime Minister's remarks in recent weeks have fuelled questions about the prospect of the UK rejoining the EU or adopting its freedom of movement rules, but he has insisted voters would ultimately be 'the boss' of any changes.
He reiterated his commitment to Labour's manifesto 'red lines' – which rule out returning to the customs union, single market or free movement – today.
'People working together in unions, trade unions, but also unions of nations, and that's what makes us who we are,' he told the conference.
'And, yes, working with the European Union, as I said, but at the same time respecting the red lines in our manifesto and respecting the referendum, the referendum result.
'So, that's the spirit, everybody, that I will take forward.'
Earlier this week, a report by a parliamentary committee warned that Mr Burnham’s plan to sign up to EU rules on food and farming will lead to an avalanche of new Brussels regulations in the UK.
The committee found that the deal is likely to require the UK to adopt ‘at least 780 pieces of EU law’ each year – equal to two new regulations every day.

SpaceX succesfully launched its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , at 5:47 p.m. EDT (2247 GMT) from Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land its Ship upper stage for the first time, but did abort a landing pad catch of its Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever recovery of an orbital Starship upper stage, if successful. See launch video above and live views from SpaceX .
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which also deployed 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

Even if you can't see SpaceX's Starship in person, you can score a model of your own. Standing at 13.77 inches (35 cm), this is a 1:375 ratio of SpaceX's Starship as a desktop model. The materials here are alloy steel and it weighs just 225g.
Ship has officially reentered Earth's atmosphere on its planned trip back to Texas' Starbase site for a historic "chopsticks" catch. The effects of our air on the vehicle are obvious; super-hot plasma now surrounds Ship's leading edges as it continues its descent.
All remains on schedule for a catch attempt around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT).
SpaceX just gave us some more information about why the Super Heavy booster aborted its chopsticks-catch try shortly after Starship's Flight 15 launch yesterday (Nov. 13).
"Early indications are that the booster ended its boostback [burn] early due to a low fuel mass alarm," SpaceX's Kate Tice said today (Nov. 14) during the company's Flight 15 webcast (which is ongoing, as Starship's Ship upper stage is currently coming back to Earth for its own catch , a milestone scheduled to occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST, 2116 GMT).
"The team is still investigating the root cause on that," Tice added. "However, booster guidance then detected that it wasn't in the right position as it was flying back, so the booster correctly aborted itself from the tower catch and went for an offshore water divert instead."
Starship 's Ship upper stage just began its descent back toward Earth. At about 3:23 p.m. EST (1823 GMT) today (Nov. 14), the vehicle conducted a 10-second, single-engine deorbit burn that went according to plan.
"Good deorbit burn," SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said during SpaceX's webcast today. "Starship [is] on its way back through the atmosphere soon."
Ship remains on target to return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT) — about 22.5 hours after it launched from the same pad on Starship's 15th test flight.
Good news, space fans: A "chopsticks" catch attempt of Starship 's Ship upper stage is officially on for this afternoon (Nov. 14).
"Moments ago, the launch team conducted the final planned contingency check for Ship's return to the launch site," SpaceX' s Kate Tice said during a webcast update today. "And, great news: All teams have polled 'go.' That included Stage 2, heat shield, flaps, structures, aero, guidance, navigation and control and, of course, the tower."
If all goes to plan, Ship will return to SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be snagged by its launch tower's arms at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), bringing an end to Starship Flight 15 , which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). SpaceX has never tried a chopsticks catch with Ship before, so tune in here at Space.com to see how it goes!
We just got some updated information about Super Heavy's landing abort during Starship Flight 15. SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot initially said that the booster diverted away from a "chopsticks" catch attempt at Starbase on Friday (Nov. 13) due to a guidance, navigation and control (GNC) issue. This morning (Nov. 14), however, he exonerated the GNC system, saying it performed as expected during Super Heavy's return to Earth.
The GNC system "detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch, did an automated abort and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location," Huot said. "The team's still digging into the root cause on how we got there, and so, more to come on that."
You can read our story about Super Heavy's landing abort here .
SpaceX is still planning to catch Starship's Ship upper stage at Starbase today. Everything looks good for that unprecedented attempt, which will occur at around 4:16 p.m. EST (2116 GMT), if all goes according to plan. You can watch it live here at Space.com.
We are now 16 hours into SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 mission , with just over six more hours remaining until the Ship 42 upper stage makes its attempted landing catch back at Starbase.
In an earlier post, I discussed SpaceX's update on how a guidance system issue caused the Super Heavy booster landing abort just after liftoff. You can now read my full story on the Super Heavy landing abort here .
Space.com's Josh Dinner captured the moment the Super Heavy booster triggered its flight termination system to explode in the Gulf of Mexico offshore from Starbase. Check it out.
Until the landing abort, the Starship Super Heavy booster performed as expected during its liftoff and stage separation, delivering its Ship upper stage to the proper position to fire its own engines and reach orbit.
Here's a stunning look at all 33 Super Heavy Raptor engines firing in unison to power the 41-story rocket's ascent into orbit, as seen by Josh.
The next Flight 15 milestone for SpaceX will be a "Final Hawaii Return Check" at the 20-hours, 41-minute mark of the mission. That will be a go/no-go moment when SpaceX decides whether to attempt the Starbase chopsticks landing at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) for Ship 42, or direct it to a splashdown off the coast of Hawaii.
Our landing livestream will begin at about that check in time, at 2 p.m. EST (1900 GMT).
Good morning and happy Saturday, Space Fans! Today is Flight Day 2 for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and SpaceX reports that its Ship 42 spacecraft is in good health as we near the 14-hour mark of its 22.5-hour test flight.
About 7 hours into the mission, SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot confirmed that flight controllers gave the go-ahead to forgo an early return window for a splashdown off the coast of Chile and proceed for the full 14-orbit flight. Starship is on track for a landing attempt, its first-ever from orbit, today (Nov. 14) at 4:20 p.m. EST (2120 GMT) . Space.com's livestream of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 landing will begin at 2 p.m. EST and you can see it at the top of this page.
"Starship's going to stay in space. We are one step closer to an eventual return to launch site," Huot said in the update. "So that's great news."
Huot also reported that Starship's tile-covered heat shield appears in good shape for today's landing attempt. SpaceX used long-range ground-based cameras and cameras on some of the 26 Starlink satellites the Ship deployed to check its heat shield after liftoff.
"Our heat shield team reviewed all the data we got from our ground tracking cameras, and from those satellite cameras and confirmed the heat shield is in a good posture for a reentry and return to the launch site," Huot said.

articles.title_orig: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.title_zh: How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA 6’ Reveals Jason And Lucia’s Limited Crime Options To Start
articles.content_orig:
Rockstar Games recently sat down to give their one-millionth interview about Grand Theft Auto 6. Not really, but it feels like that sometimes. In the interview, they discussed the open-world potential of GTA 6, which releases worldwide next week. They spoke about crime and punishment, how the characters develop alongside one another, and how you can have ’empathy’ this time around.
While talking and playing the game during the interview, Rockstar’s Rob Nelson, who is fast becoming the PR face of GTA 6, explained how the story progresses with Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the game’s co-protagonists. Like other games in the series, and in games like Red Dead, you start as a relatively small fish in a big pond.
Grand Theft Auto 6 represents the pinnacle of freedom; that much is certain. From what we’ve seen in the trailers released thus far, we’re getting a gargantuan world absolutely brimming with opportunities to explore, enjoy what’s on offer, and yes, wreak a little havoc.
But it’s not all about being a nasty criminal this time around. Rockstar recently confirmed that you can have empathy in this game for the first time in franchise history.
Rob Nelson spoke to The Guardian about the concept of crime in GTA 6, and he laid out the inner workings of the game’s story. As Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, the loved-up dual protagonists of this game, you’re not immediately able to waltz into a high-end jewelry store and make your fortune.
It’s a staggered, tiered system, it sounds like.
The interview context explains how the pair ‘can’t just steal any car or bust their way into a bank’ right out of the gate. Players will start by hotwiring low-end vehicles and picking ‘basic locks’, robbing convenience stores and gas stations before working their way up to the bigger, heftier targets.
We’ve already heard how certain cars will provide blockers to being stolen, boasting intelligent anti-theft systems, alarms, trackers, and immobilizers. We know how some store clerks will fight back, how passers-by will identify you to the police, and how people will record things on their phones, giving you a digital footprint.
It’s a fairly natural thing to assume that we wouldn’t start GTA 6 as master criminals, but in the trailers that we’ve seen thus far, we know we’re working towards that . We’ve seen Jason and Lucia robbing some pretty intense locations, decked out in body armor and wielding sophisticated weapons.
We’ve also seen them wearing Hawaiian shirts and carrying a basic handgun to empty the register in a liquor store, so the spectrum is well and truly there.
Rob Nelson explained in the interview:
These guys are a younger couple with their backs against the wall. Narratively, it doesn’t make a lot of sense for them to go out and cause as much carnage and make as much noise as they can.
Thanks to GameRoll on socials for the heads up.
Grand Theft Auto 6 is just a few days away from hitting the market. Are you looking forward to the game? Let us know your thoughts on the Insider Gaming Discord server .
For more Insider Gaming coverage, check out our interview with the developers of Azur Promilia , and don’t forget to sign up for our free weekly newsletter
Grant has been gaming for 30+ years and in the industry for 10+. You'll probably find him playing a post-apocalyptic game or an extraction shooter somewhere.

articles.title_orig: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.title_zh: Driver Stops in Front of Moving Car, Then Gets Mad When Motorist Goes Around: "Road Rage Or Insurance Scam?"
articles.content_orig:
A driver traveling on a rain-soaked road had to stop suddenly when another motorist moved into their lane and slammed on the brakes. The close call was only the start of an encounter that soon drew thousands of reactions online.
Dashcam footage shared on Reddit on November 8 shows the confrontation on a suburban road. According to the person who posted the video, the other driver came to a complete stop, leaving little room to get around.
The motorist said the other driver began yelling and making rude gestures before following their vehicle. What started as a possible rear-end crash had turned into a confrontation that continued even after the cars separated.
Now, people watching the clip are arguing over what caused the strange behavior. Some suspect road rage, while others think the driver may have been trying to cause a crash for an insurance claim.
The original Reddit post , shared by u/pooh_jo in r/dashcams, describes a drive that took an unexpected turn.
The recording begins on a wet suburban road, with other vehicles traveling nearby. As the dashcam vehicle moves forward, another car enters its lane and slows sharply before coming to a stop.
The driver behind manages to avoid hitting it, but getting past is another problem. According to the person who posted the footage, they had to reverse before there was enough space to drive around the stopped vehicle.
Rather than simply continuing down the road, the other motorist reportedly became angry. The person behind the dashcam described the driver yelling, making an obscene gesture, and later flashing their headlights while following.
The person who posted the video could not explain why the other motorist behaved that way. In the original description, they wrote, "I have no idea if this was some sort of road rage or insurance scam."
That question quickly took over the comments. One Reddit user wrote, "Honestly seems like an Insurance scam." Others agreed, pointing to the wet pavement and sudden stop as reasons for concern.
Not everyone accepted that explanation. Some commenters thought the driver might have been upset about the dashcam vehicle's speed and was trying to force it to slow down.
Another viewer suggested that a person planning an insurance scam would likely have driven away once the attempted collision failed. The continued confrontation, in that user's view, looked more like someone trying to make a point.
Neither explanation has been established. The post contains no evidence of an insurance claim or a confirmed motive for the other driver's actions.
The discussion also turned toward the person recording the footage. Several commenters questioned whether the dashcam driver was traveling too quickly for the rainy conditions.
Others pushed back, arguing that the vehicle appeared to leave enough room for nearby traffic and that the driver responded carefully to the sudden stop. One commenter claimed the posted speed was only slightly above the road's limit, though that limit has not been independently confirmed.
The argument soon shifted from the dashcam vehicle's speed to whether either driver had the right to confront another motorist over their driving.
One commenter put it simply: "Explanation doesn't equal excuse."
The person who shared the footage did not report a collision in their description. Instead, they described escaping the stopped vehicle only to have the other driver flash their lights and follow afterward.

articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.content_orig:
SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has revised its constitution to change its national flag's aspect ratio for the first time since its regime was established in 1948, according to the amended basic law posted on the website of Pyongyang's propaganda outlet.
Article 166 of the revised constitution posted on Naenara's website stipulates that the ratio of the flag's height to its width is 1 to 1.65, replacing the previous ratio of 1 to 2.
The change came as North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has sought to build his own governing style and national identity while retaining some legacies of his predecessors.
The flag's 1-to-2 ratio rule had remained unchanged in the law until the North's constitutional revision in September 2023.
Despite the ratio change, the overall design of the North's flag remains intact, consisting of a broad red stripe in the center, narrow white stripes above and below it, blue stripes above and below the white stripes, and a red five-pointed star in a white circle.
The constitution says the red stripe stands for the blood shed by anti-Japan fighters who dedicated their lives to defending the country's freedom and independence during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule. The white circle and two white stripes symbolize people's loyalty to the nation's leader and ruling Workers' Party of Korea.
The two blue stripes represent the revolutionary spirit of the people struggling for peace, friendship and unity in the world, as well as the country's sovereignty, it said.
Observers said the change in the flag's aspect ratio might have reflected Pyongyang's efforts to craft a new national image under the incumbent leader Kim, the third-generation hereditary ruler.

articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s spy scandal isn’t a one-off
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Jensen Huang and President Trump at a 2025 White House event. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
The world's most powerful AI executive admitted Sunday to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, sending shock waves through an industry built on his singular influence.
Why it matters: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has fashioned himself as the indispensable leader of an indispensable company — a $4.5 trillion behemoth with unparalleled clout in Silicon Valley, on Wall Street and inside President Trump's White House.
The big picture: Huang, who has led Nvidia since founding the chipmaker 33 years ago, has become the AI boom's chief evangelist and most authoritative voice.
Driving the news: Huang confessed to the affair in a letter to staff Sunday, apologizing to his family as Nvidia's board launched an independent probe into the suspected Chinese intelligence operation.
Zoom in: The New York Times first exposed the suspected Chinese espionage operation on Oct. 29, reporting that a woman believed to be working for Beijing had developed a close relationship with Nvidia's CEO.
The intrigue: The Trump administration reportedly knew about the suspected Chinese intelligence operation long before it became public.
Reality check: There's no public evidence that Huang's relationship influenced his advocacy for selling to China, a longstanding commercial priority for Nvidia.
What to watch: Huang's scandal comes amid a dramatic reversal of political fortunes for the AI industry, as voters rejected data center expansion and handed control of Congress to Democrats promising tougher oversight.

articles.title_orig: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.title_zh: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.content_orig:
China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents.
Two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026 reported this finding.
They also found that China holds the lion's share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.
The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.
Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability.
From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
Chinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology.
All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.
Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.
If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.
These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems.
To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.
And it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick , off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.
According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.
So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous.
The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature.
Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.
Christopher graduated from Cardiff University in 2004 with a Masters Degree in Geology. Since then, he has worked exclusively within the Built Environment, Occupational Health and Safety and Environmental Consultancy industries. He is a qualified and accredited Energy Consultant, Green Deal Assessor and Practitioner member of IEMA. Chris’s main interests range from Science and Engineering, Military and Ancient History to Politics and Philosophy.

articles.title_orig: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.title_zh: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.content_orig:
DEAR ABBY : My sister-in-law “Leah” has been a poor money manager all her life. She is in significant credit card debt and had to borrow money to help pay for her wedding, despite the fact that she has been a teacher for decades. She has never been a saver — always a spender.
When my husband passed away recently, he left me with $1 million in life insurance proceeds. When Leah found out about it (I’m not sure how), she asked me to lend her some money to get back on her feet. When I refused, my other sister-in-law chastised me, saying that my husband would have lent her the money. Leah has been bailed out a few times by her sister but never by my husband. Am I wrong to stand my ground? — NOT AN ENABLER
DEAR NOT AN ENABLER : My heart goes out to you for the loss of your husband. Leah may be using the word “lend,” but believe me when I say you would never see that money again. If she wants to get out of debt, she needs to speak to a credit counselor, not her brother’s grieving widow. If she brings it up again, tell her to visit the National Foundation for Credit Counseling at nfcc.org.
DEAR ABBY : I am a 70-year-old divorced man. For the past 10 years, my ex-wife has been living with me. Due to her medical condition and lack of family support, she has no one else to assist her. My own health is declining, so caring for her is a physical strain and emotionally stressful. She refuses any suggestion of a senior living facility because her only income is a small Social Security benefit.
How do I move on without fighting and accusations? I know I facilitated this by allowing her into my home in the first place. Any ideas where to begin? — FRUSTRATED IN TEXAS
DEAR FRUSTRATED : You were kind to take in and care for your ex a decade ago, but this arrangement is now affecting your health. To protect your own well-being, you must put your foot down. Help your ex-wife one last time by finding her a facility she can afford. Do not expect the transition to be pleasant, but the result will be an improvement for both of you.
DEAR ABBY : I am a happily married woman who went through a midlife crisis more than 20 years ago. At the time, I left my husband for another man, who gave me an expensive cocktail ring. When my relationship with the new man started to suffer for various reasons, I returned to my husband. Our marriage has remained strong ever since.
I have never worn the ring and have always felt guilty for having it. Should I contact my former lover and return it? Should I pawn it and send him the proceeds? Or maybe you have another suggestion? — RINGS HOLLOW IN ARIZONA
DEAR RINGS HOLLOW : Sell the ring and donate the proceeds to a worthy charitable cause. Do not open the door to further contact with your former lover.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at http://www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

articles.title_orig: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.title_zh: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's now ex-CEO left the post after it emerged he was romantically involved with a woman alleged to be spying for China, jolting the U.S. AI surge and thrusting allegations of Chinese penetration at major Western tech firms into the spotlight .
Beijing rejected the claims as a smear and said Washington is inventing "Chinese spy narratives" to rationalize curbs on technology exports. Even so, the operative suspected of involvement in the episode that precipitated Huang 's exit is currently in China and the Chinese government is aware of her presence.
What hangs in the balance is economic and military clout. The U.S. is betting a lead in AI and advanced chips will sustain its strength and help deter China over Taiwan, while espionage offers Beijing a way to narrow that lead and glean insight into U.S. military plans and political decision-making.
German prosecutors report that a married pair posed as interpreters and auto-sector workers to court academics across AI, computer science and aerospace, flying some to China to give paid "civilian" talks for state-owned defense companies.
According to New Zealand intelligence, a Chinese observatory closely linked to the government attempted to set up space-tracking gear via a domestic firm, equipment that might double as a tool for gathering military intelligence. Taiwan says Chinese agents trawl social media to find soldiers in debt, extend loans, and then demand sensitive information and referrals to fellow service members.
The Philippines offers a closer look at scale and sophistication. Authorities say suspected Chinese operatives claimed they flew drones loaded with fishing bait while observing warships near Subic Bay, and that another group pretended to be seafood purchasers as they piloted drones close to a naval installation. In Manila, contracted drivers equipped their cars with sham cellphone towers and cruised by the presidential palace, military encampments and the U.S. Embassy to scoop up nearby phone data.
A separate car outfitted with cameras plus mapping gear made stops at more than 120 sites, among them bases used by American forces. Officials add that presumed operatives cultivated sources within the defense establishment to secure rosters of naval personnel, timetables for troop rotations and resupply, and details on missions to outposts in the disputed South China Sea.
An investigator told Bloomberg the network encompassed hundreds. China has rejected the allegations as baseless.
In uncertain times, thoughtful investors look for reliable ways to sharpen their edge. We're hosting our first ever investor livestream on 11/17 to show you how to use ChatGPT and Claude to invest like a pro, hosted by Briefs Finance CEO Jaspreet Singh. Save your seat .
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the activity is widespread and not confined to the Philippines, pointing to cases in the United States, Australia and the United Kingdom.
Security agencies are turning up the volume. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Chinese espionage is "a grave threat to the economic well-being" of the U.S. Britain's MI5 reported that in 2022 it was handling seven times the number of China-related probes as it had four years before. Canadian intelligence describes China as its "greatest counter-intelligence threat," while Dutch intelligence reports that Chinese digital espionage targeting technology firms is occurring on a "large scale."
China's Ministry of State Security is central to this push, combining overseas and domestic roles and, under Xi Jinping, tightening control over local bureaus to coordinate nationwide and pursue more ambitious missions abroad. Under the 2017 National Intelligence Law, every organization and citizen must "support, assist, and cooperate" with intelligence work.
Holden Triplett, who once led the FBI's Beijing office, said Chinese services have become highly professional, increasingly exploit human vulnerabilities, and that anyone can be susceptible.
With the AI revolution in full swing, Western officials say Chinese spy agencies have prioritized the technology that underpins it, seeking it through hacking and human sources.
AI is also changing tradecraft. "Human espionage doesn't anymore have to be sneaking around back alleys."
AI is also boosting cyber operations.
The bottom line: Washington is counting on AI and advanced chips to preserve economic and military heft, and the alleged espionage drive aims at those very advantages.

articles.title_orig: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.title_zh: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: Setback for SpaceX reusable rocket system despite successful launch
articles.title_zh: Setback for SpaceX reusable rocket system despite successful launch
articles.content_orig:
US company SpaceX has successfully launched the latest flight of its Starship spacecraft into orbit but did not recover the booster rocket as planned.
The company, owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk , is hoping to develop a fully reusable rocket system. It had planned to recover both the booster and the upper stage, which is the spacecraft itself.
Instead of landing back at the launch site, the booster exploded above the Gulf of Mexico. The upper stage is currently in orbit and the plan is to recover it on Saturday when it returns to Earth.
It is to be caught by mechanical arms upon landing back at the launch pad, marking the first time the spacecraft would be caught after returning to Earth. It could then potentially be reused in the future.
In addition to testing the reusable rocket system, the mission also delivered 26 of SpaceX’s satellites for its Starlink network .
SpaceX's Starship is the world's largest and most powerful rocket system. At 124 meters (407 feet) tall, it consists of a spacecraft mounted on a booster rocket. Both stages were designed from the outset to be fully reusable.
At the launch, both the spacecraft and booster successfully lifted off from the SpaceX South Texas Starbase site. While the Friday launch was an uncrewed mission, Starship is designed to carry both crew and cargo.
On its return path, the booster diverted from its flight path to the launch site and steered to a designated area over the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded over the sea surface. The reasons for the failure of the controlled landing were not immediately clear.
"Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said.
The upper stage continued into orbit and soon after began releasing the 26 satellites it was carrying.
It is scheduled to return to Earth on Saturday.
Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.
In previous launches, the Starship booster was successfully recovered. The upper stages of the 14 previous Starship missions have all ended up in the ocean though, either by design or because of failures .
The new objective of Friday’s launch was to recover both stages of the Starship launch system.
Currently, SpaceX is mostly using smaller Falcon rockets, which are not fully reusable because the second stage cannot be recovered.
Musk said he expected SpaceX to conduct Starship launches once a week by early 2027.
The project has received billions of dollars in NASA funding, with SpaceX also investing at least $15 billion.
The main goal of the program is to put astronauts on the Moon by 2028 although outstanding technical challenges could delay that schedule.

articles.title_orig: Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China’s Xi, US officials say
articles.title_zh: Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China’s Xi, US officials say
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX launches milestone Starship flight to demonstrate full reusability of orbit-class rocket
articles.title_zh: SpaceX launches milestone Starship flight to demonstrate full reusability of orbit-class rocket
articles.content_orig:
In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.
The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.
Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.
Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.
In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.
When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."
Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month .
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

articles.title_orig: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
His comments come as some of President Donald Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump himself has also fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisors raising alarm bells about Lutnick, two additional people said.
So far, the White House has stood by him, issuing a statement Thursday – before Bessent’s comments – saying Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Trump and Lutnick are longtime friends, and sources said it was unclear what the president might do.
Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing Megaspeed on an export blacklist.
He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed the follow through.
“Commerce…has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
He suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump.
“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, he said.
“And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage,” he went on.
CNN has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks.
But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when it was reported publicly that Huang had an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of having intelligence connections to China.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive.
Despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, people familiar with the matter said.
In a tense Situation Room meeting last week, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed, CNN previously reported. Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
In the interview Friday, Bessent did not deny the confrontation .
“We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” he said.

articles.title_zh: Donald Trump will not raise Nvidia spy issue with Xi Jinping at summit, officials say
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."
